## DAILY SECURITY BRIEFING

### 1. Russia mounts major missile and drone attack on Kyiv
Russia launched 168 drones alongside cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles against Ukraine, with Kyiv and the surrounding region the main target. At least 15 people were killed—some reports put the toll at 17—and more than 40 injured. Residential buildings, a school, kindergarten, children’s hospital and critical infrastructure were damaged.

**Why it matters:** Ukraine intercepted most drones and cruise missiles, but remains vulnerable to ballistic weapons. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said delayed replenishment of Patriot interceptors was costing lives, while the EU identified anti-ballistic support as an urgent priority.

### 2. Ukraine expands deep strikes against Russian energy and military infrastructure
Ukraine reported attacks on the Taneco refinery in Tatarstan, the Tamanneftegaz terminal, airfields used to launch Russian drones, and infrastructure supplying occupied Crimea. Russia has confirmed importing gasoline after Ukrainian strikes disrupted refineries and depots, with shipments arriving from India and additional imports being arranged from Belarus and Kazakhstan.

**Why it matters:** The campaign is affecting Russia’s domestic fuel supply and its former status as a peacetime fuel exporter. It also demonstrates Ukraine’s growing long-range strike capability as both sides intensify attacks far behind the front.

### 3. Russian attacks generate further security incidents on NATO’s eastern flank
Romania destroyed an explosive-laden naval drone near the Neptun Deep Black Sea gas platform after officials said Kyiv confirmed it was not Ukrainian. A separate aerial drone entered Romanian airspace and crashed in an unpopulated area, while Poland activated aircraft and air defences during the Russian barrage. Moldova also reported drone-related incidents.

**Why it matters:** Repeated incursions and debris falls increase the risk of escalation or miscalculation involving NATO territory and critical energy infrastructure. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the broader pattern as an escalating hybrid threat.

### 4. North Korea fires missiles despite reduced US–South Korean exercises
North Korea launched around 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area, with each flying approximately 300 kilometres. The launches followed President Donald Trump’s decision to shorten the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises and his statement that he expected to meet Kim Jong Un later this year. Pyongyang dismissed the reduction as insufficient while saying the leaders’ personal relationship remained “excellent.”

**Why it matters:** The launch indicates that the US concession has not produced immediate military restraint. It also comes amid deepening North Korean-Russian defence cooperation; Ukrainian intelligence separately claims Russia has received North Korean KN-30 ballistic missiles.

### 5. Washington threatens a broader economic campaign against Iran
Trump announced plans for intensified economic isolation of Iran, including possible consequences for third countries that facilitate Iranian trade or financial access. Tehran rejected the threat, while an Iranian lawmaker called for withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

**Why it matters:** The move could widen pressure on Iran’s trading partners and further complicate stalled negotiations. Iranian debate over leaving the NPT raises additional proliferation concerns, although no formal withdrawal was announced.

## WATCH

- **Ukraine’s Patriot supply:** Whether the US and European partners rapidly provide interceptors as Russia increases ballistic attacks and targets energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
- **Black Sea and NATO airspace incidents:** Attribution of the Romanian naval drone and whether further incursions prompt changes to NATO force posture or rules of engagement.
- **US–North Korea diplomacy:** Whether a Trump–Kim meeting is arranged and whether Pyongyang seeks larger concessions while continuing missile tests.

### North Korea Fires Short-Range Ballistic-Missile Barrage

North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area toward its eastern waters. South Korea said they flew approximately 300 kilometers and convened an emergency security meeting; Seoul, Washington and Tokyo increased coordination and surveillance.

**Why it matters:** The launches violate U.N. Security Council restrictions and demonstrate North Korea’s ability to threaten targets across South Korea. They also sustain military pressure despite renewed U.S. diplomatic overtures.

### Washington Scales Back Allied Drills, but Pyongyang Rejects Overture

President Donald Trump ordered the annual U.S.-South Korean Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise shortened and reduced, citing his relationship with Kim Jong Un and an interest in renewed talks. Trump said he expected to meet Kim later this year. Kim Yo Jong denied knowledge of current leader-level communication and said reducing the drills did not change what Pyongyang considers their hostile character. South Korean ministries reportedly received no advance explanation of the U.S. decision.

**Why it matters:** The move could reopen diplomacy, but Pyongyang appears to be seeking larger concessions before engaging. The limited consultation and reduced training have also raised concerns about alliance coordination and combined military readiness.

### Allies Train Against North Korea’s Expanding Drone Threat

U.S. and South Korean forces held their first Osan Air Base counter-drone drills focused on medium-sized Group 3 systems. The exercise used simulated hostile drones and involved U.S. Air Force, Army and Marine Corps air-defense systems. North Korea is reportedly developing one-way attack drones based on Iranian and Russian designs.

**Why it matters:** Relatively inexpensive attack drones could threaten aircraft, personnel and infrastructure at major allied bases. The training reflects an effort to close a potential air-defense gap between protection against small drones and conventional missile threats.

### WATCH

- **Prospects for a Trump-Kim meeting:** Monitor whether Pyongyang demands additional reductions in exercises or other concessions before agreeing to talks.
- **Regional nuclear posture:** South Korea estimates North Korea may possess 80–120 nuclear warheads, while China and Russia are warning against any weakening of Japan’s non-nuclear policy.

### 1. Large Russian barrage exposes Ukraine’s ballistic-defence gap

Russia launched a major combined attack on Kyiv and surrounding areas using ballistic and cruise missiles, Banderol loitering munitions and 168 drones. At least 15 people were reported killed, with later accounts putting the toll at 17; homes, schools, a children’s hospital and infrastructure were damaged. Ukraine reported intercepting most cruise missiles and drones but did not confirm comparable success against ballistic weapons.

**Why it matters:** The attack demonstrates Russia’s ability to combine different weapon types to strain Ukrainian air defences. Kyiv says shortages of Patriot interceptors—the principal Ukrainian system capable of defeating ballistic missiles—are leaving cities and military-industrial facilities increasingly vulnerable.

### 2. Ukrainian strikes deepen pressure on Russia’s fuel sector

Ukraine reported strikes on the Taneco refinery in Tatarstan, the Tamanneftegaz Black Sea terminal, drone-launch airfields and a power substation serving occupied Crimea. Russia, normally a gasoline exporter, has begun importing fuel from India and is arranging additional supplies from Belarus and Kazakhstan. Moscow has also restricted fuel exports.

**Why it matters:** The shift to imports indicates that Ukrainian attacks on refineries and depots are affecting Russia’s domestic fuel market. Continued disruption could increase costs, tighten supplies in Russia and occupied territories, and place additional pressure on regional fuel markets.

### 3. War-related threats spread across the EU and NATO eastern flank

Romania destroyed an explosive-laden naval drone near the Neptun Deep offshore gas platform and reported an aerial drone incident on its territory. Romanian officials said Kyiv had denied that the naval drone was Ukrainian, although its origin was not independently established. Moldova also reported a suspected drone incursion, while Poland and Romania activated aircraft and air defences during the Russian barrage.

**Why it matters:** These incidents increase risks to NATO territory, civilian populations and critical Black Sea energy infrastructure. They also reinforce European concerns about hybrid threats and highlight gaps in eastern-flank air and missile defence.

### WATCH

- **North Korean missile support:** Ukrainian intelligence says Russia has received KN-30 ballistic missiles and that North Korea is deploying a missile unit in Russia’s Voronezh region. Operational use or independent confirmation would mark a further expansion of Moscow-Pyongyang military cooperation.
- **Winter escalation:** Monitor Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy system and whether Western partners accelerate deliveries of Patriot interceptors and other anti-ballistic capabilities.

## 1. US intensifies military and economic pressure on Iran

**What happened:** President Donald Trump announced an expanded campaign to isolate Iran economically, threatening consequences for countries, financial institutions and companies that facilitate Iranian trade. Specific new measures were not disclosed. Meanwhile, the USS *George Washington* arrived in the Middle East to replace the long-deployed USS *Abraham Lincoln* and joined the USS *George H.W. Bush*. The US Navy continues to enforce restrictions on Iranian ports around the Strait of Hormuz.

**Why it matters:** The combination of threatened secondary sanctions, port restrictions and a sustained two-carrier presence signals continued pressure despite a recent reduction in hostilities. It could disrupt Iranian oil and commercial networks, affect Tehran’s trading partners and increase the risk of renewed confrontation around the Strait of Hormuz.

## 2. Israeli strike highlights tensions over Turkey’s role in Syria

**What happened:** Israel struck Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase after alleging that Damascus was preparing to permit a Turkish military deployment there. Turkey denied having a military presence at the base and said it was not considering retaliation. Separately, sources reported that Mossad chief Roman Gofman and Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani discussed Turkish military activity and arms supplies four days before the strike.

**Why it matters:** The episode underscores growing Israeli concern about Turkish influence in post-Assad Syria. Continued Israeli attacks intended to restrict Turkish military access could complicate Syria’s stabilization, undermine emerging Israel-Syria security contacts and create friction between Israel and Turkey.

## 3. Gaza ceasefire comes under renewed strain

**What happened:** Two Israeli airstrikes in Gaza City killed at least 15 Palestinians within 24 hours, according to Palestinian medical sources, including nine people at a Hamas-run municipal police headquarters. The attacks occurred while US, Egyptian and Qatari mediators were seeking progress toward the ceasefire’s second phase. Talks remain stalled over Israeli withdrawal, Hamas’s weapons and Gaza’s future governance and security.

**Why it matters:** Renewed strikes increase the risk that the fragile ceasefire will collapse. Failure to resolve the central political and security disputes could restart wider fighting and further obstruct humanitarian access and postwar planning.

## WATCH

- **Iraqi militia disarmament:** An unidentified armed faction reportedly transferred about 20 Iranian-made attack drones and longer-range missiles to the Iraqi government under US observation. Major Iran-aligned factions continue to reject disarmament, raising the possibility of sanctions or an internal confrontation.
- **Russia-Iran technology links:** An investigation alleges that nuclear-related expertise may have accompanied Russian payments for Iranian drone support. The evidence remains circumstantial but warrants monitoring for indications of sensitive technology transfer.

### 1. U.S. Army explores long-term HAWK sustainment contract
The Army issued a Sources Sought notice to identify contractors capable of providing comprehensive logistics, engineering, maintenance and materiel support for the HAWK missile system. Responses are due on September 2, 2026, but the notice does not commit the Army to awarding a contract.

**Why it matters:** The move indicates continued U.S. planning to sustain a legacy air-defense system that is no longer in U.S. Army service but remains operational abroad.

### 2. Support would cover Ukraine and other partner nations
The proposed work would support HAWK systems operated through Foreign Military Sales and partner-capacity programs, including systems supplied to Ukraine since late 2022.

**Why it matters:** Reliable maintenance, testing and missile support are necessary to keep partner-operated HAWK batteries available for air and missile defense. The requirement also underscores the U.S. role in supporting older equipment transferred to allies.

### 3. Scope includes broader air-defense integration
The contemplated contract includes integration support involving Sentinel radars, NASAMS and short-range air-defense systems. Major support and testing activities would be centered at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico and associated partner-country facilities.

**Why it matters:** Integration could help partner nations operate HAWK within layered air-defense networks rather than as a stand-alone system. White Sands would remain a central hub for testing, readiness monitoring and technical support.

### WATCH
- Whether the Army proceeds from market research to a formal solicitation and contract award.
- The extent to which new sustainment arrangements improve HAWK readiness in Ukraine and other partner countries.

articles.title: Russia launches ‘massive attack’ on Kyiv and surrounding region – Europe live
articles.body:
EU's von der Leyen warns of 'escalating campaign of threats' against the bloc after Romania destroys naval drone near gas platform
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyencriticised “an escalating campaign of threats” against the European Union, as she responded to Romania’s decision to destroy a naval drone near its Neptun Deep platform in the Black Sea (12:33).
“An escalating campaign of threats is underway, unsettling our citizens and seeking to divide our Union. This is hybrid warfare,” she said, without naming the aggressor.
She continued:
“The founding mission of our Union is to preserve peace. Today, that also means having the capacity to deter provocation and aggression. Our Readiness 2030 agenda is mobilising up to EUR 800 billion.
With the European Drone Defence Initiative and the Eastern Flank Watch, we are scaling up production in Europe to deliver capabilities Member States need. So we can respond to emerging threats with speed, unity and resolve.”
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyencriticised “an escalating campaign of threats” against the European Union, after Romania discovered a naval drone “loaded with explosive” near its Neptun Deep platform in the Black Sea (13:50).
Romanian defence minister Radu Miruță said the decision was taken “to protect the lives of the several hundred people working on the platform and to secure the critical infrastructure” (12:33).
Miruță added that Romanian officials confirmed with Kyiv that the vessel was “not of Ukrainian origin,” strongly suggesting Russian involvement amid heightened tensions in the region.
Separately,
A heavy Russian missile and drone bombardment has killed at least 15 people in and around Kyiv in one of the most intense aerial attacks on Ukraine’s capital since the start of the war (9:35).
The attack highlighted Ukraine’s vulnerability to ballistic missiles as Kyiv continues to call on the US and European partners to supply them with more interceptors (14:21, 14:54).
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Russia running on imported gasoline, government confirms
Russia has begun importing fuel, its government has confirmed, as a shipload of gasoline arrived from India.
A fuel exporter in peacetime, Russia has been forced to turn to imports after Ukrainian strikes on its refineries and depots in response to the Russian invasion.
The campaign by Kyiv’s military has been a major success, causing fuel shortages across Russia and in illegally occupied Crimea.
At least one cargo of gasoline from India has just entered Russia’s domestic market, three industry sources told Reuters and shipping data showed.
Russia is also arranging rail imports of gasoline from Belarus and Kazakhstan, and has placed a ban on fuel exports.
Reuters reported last week that Russia had also begun shipping in diesel from Asia.
Ukraine is struggling to defend itself from high-speed ballistics - snap analysis
Dan Sabbagh
Defence and security editor
A shortage of Patriot interceptors means that Ukraine is struggling to defend itself from attack from high-speed ballistics, which can arrive within minutes of an air raid warning.
Earlier this month the air force decided to stop announcing how many ballistics had been launched, citing security concerns.
Both sides have been escalating long-range attacks while air defences remain short. Ukraine has attacked oil refineries and warehouses close to Moscow using newly developed cruise missiles and drones, while Russia has stepped up its attacks on Kyiv, making heavy use of hard ballistics.
Ukraine's partners 'cannot simply watch silently and indifferently' as Russia 'destroy lives,' Zelenskyy says in dramatic appeal for missile interceptors
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said “more than 600 first responders” are still involved in responding to the overnight Russian attacks on Kyiv, which killed 15 people.
“It is important that Ukraine’s partners do not remain silent about this and other similar strikes and truly help protect our people, protect life in Ukraine. This Russian strike was one of the most cynical, calculated, and large-scale. There were various types of missiles and 168 drones,” he said.
Zelenskyy warned that ballistic missiles remain “the biggest threat,” as Ukraine suffers from shortage of missile interceptors.
“This is something that depends entirely on the supply of Patriot missiles to Ukraine and therefore depends on our country’s partners. You cannot simply watch silently and indifferently, doing nothing as the Russians destroy lives with ballistic missiles.”

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyencriticised “an escalating campaign of threats” against the European Union, as she responded to Romania’s decision to destroy a naval drone near its Neptun Deep platform in the Black Sea (12:33).
“An escalating campaign of threats is underway, unsettling our citizens and seeking to divide our Union. This is hybrid warfare,” she said, without naming the aggressor.
She continued:
“The founding mission of our Union is to preserve peace. Today, that also means having the capacity to deter provocation and aggression. Our Readiness 2030 agenda is mobilising up to EUR 800 billion.
With the European Drone Defence Initiative and the Eastern Flank Watch, we are scaling up production in Europe to deliver capabilities Member States need. So we can respond to emerging threats with speed, unity and resolve.”
Romania destroys marine drone spotted near major offshore gas project
Romania’s military has destroyed a marine drone spotted just “a few hundred meters” from the Neptun Deep platform, a major offshore gas project in the Black Sea.
The drone, spotted just “a few hundreds of meters” from the gas extraction works at the Neptun Deep platform located some 80 miles east of the city of Constanța, was destroyed by a Romanian F-16 fighter jet.
“Following the analyses carried out and in coordination with the President of Romania, in order to protect the lives of the several hundred people working on the platform and to secure the critical infrastructure, the decision was made to destroy the drone,” Romania’s defence minister Radu Miruță said in a post on Facebook.
Miruță added that Romanian officials confirmed with Kyiv that the vessel was “not of Ukrainian origin,” strongly suggesting Russian involvement amid heightened maritime tensions in the region.
Earlier this month, Romanian army divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones drifting in the country’s Black Sea exclusive economic zone near the same offshore gas project.
Ukraine faces 'terror that is only growing' from Russia, former army chief says
Ukraine’s UK ambassador and former army chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi also called for Ukraine to get “not word, but concrete help from partners,” as he warned that country faced “terror that is only growing” from Russia.
Russia testing Nato's resolve with airspace incidents in neighbouring countries, Ukraine's minister warns
Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said that Russia violated the airspace of Moldova and Romania during last night’s attacks on Ukraine.
“These are not isolated incidents. They are part of Russia’s deliberate and systemic terrorist attacks. The aggressor state is increasingly testing the resolve of Nato and its partners, violating the sovereignty of neighbouring states and deliberately expanding the risks posed by its war far beyond Ukraine,” he warned.
Sybiha said he would work with his counterparts in both countries “toward a stronger and more effective regional response to Russia’s cynical attempts to widen the war it started.”
“Our collective response must be stronger than Russia’s attempts to test our unity and resolve. The security and stability of the entire region are at stake,” he said.
A children’s hospital was struck in the Solomianskyi district to the west of the heart of the capital, with windows blown out and cars burned. At least two residential buildings were also reported hit in the area.
Explosions could be heard from the city centre at about midnight on Wednesday, earlier than the normal timing of Russian missile strikes, and there was a further wave of attacks early on Thursday morning.
An attack in Brovary district of the broader Kyiv region killed one man and wounded another, said the regional governor, Tymur Tkachenko. “One industrial facility has been damaged. All relevant services are on site, working to extinguish the fire,” he said.
Ukraine’s air force had warned of Russian Kalibr cruise missiles passing over the regional village of Kaharlyk and heading towards the capital.
Russia-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant loses external power supply
The United Nations nuclear watchdog said on Thursday that Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station lost its only remaining external power line, forcing emergency diesel generators to start supplying vital safety systems, Reuters reported.
The International Atomic Energy Agency, or IAEA, said on X that initial assessment indicated the damage was located on the northern bank of the Dnipro River, and technicians were unable to determine the outage’s cause due to military activity.
The plant, Europe’s largest with six reactors, produces no electricity but needs power supplied by two external links to keep nuclear fuel cool, Reuters said.
Ukraine’s air force said that Russia had launched dozens of ballistic, cruise, and hypersonic missiles, as well as 168 drones in its overnight attack on the country.
It said that air defence units downed 145 drones and most of the cruise missiles but none of the missiles that run on ballistic trajectory, Reuters said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has for month been pushing for more anti-ballistic missiles to be delivered to Ukraine.
18 people hospitalised after overnight attacks on Kyiv
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said 18 people have been hospitalised after the overnight attacks, with emergency and clean-up response continuing at various sites across three districts of the city.
“The capital is recovering from a massive enemy attack,” he said in a video on Telegram.
“Residential and non-residential buildings, a school, and a children’s hospital were damaged,” he added.
At least 12 people were killed and 40 injured in a series of Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv.
“It was a massive attack – the Russians had been preparing for a long time, combining different types of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones, aiming to cause as much damage as possible to civilian infrastructure. There is destruction in Kyiv and the region, as well as in the Odesa and Chernihiv regions,” Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
The attack will likely draw further attention to Ukraine’s shortage of air defence missiles.
“While Moscow is investing in ballistic missiles and escalation, such strikes do not always receive the response they should from the world. And as long as Ukraine does not have enough anti-ballistic defence, Russia will not consider peace seriously,” Zelenskyy warned this morning.
Pledging with allies to send more Patriot interceptors to help protect Ukraine, he stressed that “every additional missile saves the lives of our people.”
More drone attack warnings from Kyiv were going live this morning.
Responding to the overnight attacks, Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko declared Friday a day of mourning in the city.
I will bring you more updates throughout the day.
It’s Thursday, 20 August 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: Osan Drills Target North Korea’s Growing Drone Threat
articles.body:
Some 50 miles from the border with North Korea, U.S. and South Korean forces recently executed their first counter-drone defense drills targeting medium-sized systems, which the North Korean military has has prioritized based on Russia and Iranian models.
Airmen, Soldiers, and Marines conducted exercise Dragon Flight from Aug. 2-6 at Osan Air Base, according to a 51st Fighter Wing release. The drills were conducted before President Donald Trump scaled back the recent larger, peninsula-wide, annual Ulchi Freedom Shield.
The exercise helped service members practice defending the F-16C/D fighters at Osan, which in turn defend against threats such as North Korea. The base’s primary mission is to launch waves of fighter jets in a potential conflict.
“This exercise helped all the involved agencies assess and validate their respective C-UAS defense systems,” 1st Lt. Thu Le with the 51st Security Forces Squadron said in the release. “I hope that this event gives the 51st Fighter Wing confidence in its current air defense capabilities and just shows how crucial such systems are to the defense of the base, its assets, and all 16,000 joint-force personnel.”
The exercise gave Osan a chance to train on a portion of air defense it hasn’t always focused on: Group 3 drones. These systems fall between smaller Group 1 and 2 threats and larger, legacy ballistic missiles, both of which personnel at Osan and Kunsan Air Bases have trained to defeat.
Alongside the service members conducting the counter-drone training were contractors from Griffin Aerospace, which operated the Outlaw Drone to simulate hostile aircraft.
Members of the 51st Security Forces Squadron used the Expeditionary Mobile Air Defense System to beat back the threat.
Soldiers with the 35th Air Defense Brigade used the AN/TWQ Avenger system while Marines with the 2nd Low Altitude Air Defense Battalion used Stinger man-portable missiles with Smart Shooter SMASH optics, according to the release.
Republic of Korea personnel also worked in the exercise with their own equipment.
The Bigger Picture
This training comes as U.S. bases and forward-deployed units face an ever-increasing drone threat, especially from Group 3 drones, which weigh between 50 and 1,320 pounds, fly up to 18,000 feet at speeds under 250 knots, and cost between $20,000 and $50,000 to produce.
During Operation Epic Fury, Iran has launched an estimated 2,000 Shahed-136 drones, which are Group 3, at U.S. and allied forces in the region, forcing the U.S. to use expensive munitions to take them down.
An Iranian one-way drone hit a U.S. facility in the Port of Shuaiba, Kuwait, on June 1, killing six U.S. soldiers.
Russia has used Iranian technology to build its own one-way attack drones, and North Korea has contributed troops and weapons to Russia in its war against Ukraine. In turn, Russia has reportedly helped North Korea to copy the Shahed and begin building factory lines to produce the knockoffs in 2025. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has called drone production an “essential requirement” and a “top priority and important task” for modernizing the nation’s military.
Prior to the Shahed focus, North Korea used its own drones to conduct perimeter incursions into the Demilitarized Zone between North and South Korea in December 2022.
Since then, local news reports say smaller reconnaissance drones have been spotted in South Korean border cities from 2024 to 2025.
While both Osan and Kunsan Air Bases in South Korea have MIM-104 Patriot Systems for ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and fighter jets, as well as short-range air defense systems such as the AN/TWQ Avenger system, those are mainly geared toward low-altitude aircraft, cruise missiles, and helicopters.
Kunsan has not yet conducted a specific counter-drone exercise for Group 3 drones. However, Kunsan personnel have conducted exercises such as Beverley Sentinel, using red teams to test defenses against Group 1 and 2 drones.

articles.title: Russia Received KN-30 Ballistic Missiles From North Korea — Defence Intelligence of Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia has received KN-30 ballistic missiles supplied by North Korea, which could be used to strike Ukraine.
This is according to data from the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, which the agency provided in response to a request from Ukrainska Pravda media outlet.
According to the intelligence service, as of July 2026, Russia had around 50 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles and approximately the same number of North Korean KN-23, KN-24 and KN-30 ballistic missiles.
There had been no previous reports of KN-30 missiles being transferred to Russia or used in the war against Ukraine. Russia has used North Korean KN-23 and KN-24 missiles in strikes.
The KN-30 is the Western designation for the North Korean Hwasong-11C ballistic missile, also known as the Hwasong-11Da. It is an enlarged version of the Hwasong-11 family and belongs to the short-range ballistic missile class.
The missile is powered by a solid-fuel engine and launched from a mobile ground-based launcher.
The first known test launch of the Hwasong-11C took place on March 25, 2021. During the test, the missile demonstrated a range of at least 600 kilometers.
North Korea claimed that the missile could carry a 2.5-ton warhead. However, this information has not been independently confirmed.
The KN-30 was first publicly displayed at a military parade in Pyongyang on January 14, 2021.
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine also provided information on the Russian military’s stockpiles of other missiles. As of August 5, the stockpile of 9M723 ballistic missiles for Iskander-M operational-tactical missile systems allocated to Russia’s military grouping stood at around 130.
Russia is estimated to have around 400 RM-48U missiles for S-400 air defense systems. It also has more than 600 Oniks anti-ship missiles, more than 450 Kalibr cruise missiles, more than 120 Zircon hypersonic missiles and up to 100 Kh-101 cruise missiles.
In early August, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine representative Andrii Cherniak said that North Korea had begun deploying a missile unit in Russia’s Voronezh region to launch ballistic missile strikes against Ukraine.

articles.title: Mecca Defence Pact marks the start of a post-American Arab Gulf
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Mecca Defence Pact marks the start of a post-American Arab Gulf
Saudi figures put the number of Iranian missiles and drones fired towards the kingdom by late March at more than 700. Washington had launched the war alongside Israel a month earlier, yet Saudi air defences did most of the intercepting, and Riyadh spent the following months protecting its cities and oil infrastructure.
The American security guarantee in the Gulf broke when Saudi air defences took over, not when the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement was signed on 7 August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. The deal is often cited as evidence that the US-led order has ended, but in reality, it is paperwork that arrived four months late.
The retrenchment it supposedly announces has been underway since 2008. The financial crisis, the exhaustion of Iraq and Afghanistan and the turn towards competition with China pushed Washington away from occupation and towards sanctions, airpower and financial coercion. It is a model of regime management that imposes outcomes on other states while avoiding the cost of holding their territory.
The second pillar is burden-shifting, pressing partners to absorb the frontline costs of American strategy while Washington keeps the escalation umbrella. The Abraham Accords were its most over-engineered expression, trying to lock in regional enforcement through Israel that most Gulf states refused to join.
Set against that strategy, three states arming themselves while keeping their American relationships intact is not a rupture but a result. Turkey remains in NATO and continues to press for F-35s. Pakistan has spent this war as Washington’s channel to Tehran. And nine days before the ceremony in Mecca, Saudi Arabia flew joint strikes with US Central Command against Iran-aligned militias in Iraq.
A pact whose members are simultaneously fighting beside American forces, brokering for American diplomacy and shopping for American aircraft is not the end of an order; it is that order economising. In reality, it adds little to what the war had already shown. What matters is how it is being read in Tehran, and by whom.
The reading from Iran’s ruling bloc
The memorandum of understanding that preceded this summer’s fighting was engineered by Iran’s actual ruling class. This is the bloc organised around the Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), the wider security establishment, the revolutionary-religious foundations (bonyads) that control much of the economy, and the Office of the Supreme Leader, which appoints their leadership and shields them from oversight.
Indeed, the bloc is not monolithic: a technocratic-economic wing holds that the Islamic Republic survives through economic recovery rather than ideological performance, while an ideological-maximalist wing, centred on the Paydari Front, regards engagement with Washington as futile.
The technocratic wing is in command, and its authority rests on institutions rather than personalities. When the truce collapsed on 8 July, it pushed Iran back into war rather than abandoning diplomacy, on the calculation that without control of Hormuz, Iran has nothing to sell when it returns to the table.
Its response to Mecca has been to shrink it. The IRGC-linked press warned negotiators against conceding anything, fearing a coalition that has not yet formed, because “the first defeat can occur not in war, but in the mind”. Other media outlets with similar political affiliations cited technical grounds: no joint command, no common fund, no automatic trigger.
The maximalists dissented, blaming President Masoud Pezeshkian for diplomacy too absorbed in Washington to see the pact coming, but they are weaker than their volume suggests.
More telling is what the security establishment was doing in the same days. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei appointed six senior commanders, installing Ahmad Vahidi as commander of the Revolutionary Guards and tasking the new chief of the Armed Forces General Staff with folding that body into the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, Iran’s wartime joint command. Days later, Mohsen Rezaei, who had run the Guards for 16 years, took over the Supreme National Security Council.
Some read this as the leadership clipping the technocratic wing; it overreads a single appointment, since Rezaei comes from the same establishment and the week’s direction was consolidation rather than redistribution.
The reshuffle shows a certain disposition. A bloc that folds its general staff into a wartime command does not see a defence pact among neighbours as its main problem. It has already adjusted to a region where Washington no longer guarantees outcomes. Its strategy was built for this reality.
A danger that needs no clause
On the narrow question, the bloc is likely correct. The collective defence article will not bring Turkish or Pakistani soldiers into a war with Iran. But the pact does not need to operate militarily to harm Iran. Here, composure becomes a risk.
The first exposure is political, and it builds over time. Iran’s neighbours are forming regional arrangements without it. Erdogan has said that Egypt could join. Each new member makes the next step easier and less costly to dismiss Iranian objections.
The second is economic, and no longer hypothetical. Twenty years of sanctions have produced an economy whose lifelines run overland and through re-export hubs, and the three that matter are Turkey, Pakistan and, above all, the United Arab Emirates.
On 18 August, after two Iranian ballistic missiles were fired towards its territory, Abu Dhabi suspended all trade and financial transactions with Iran until further notice. In one announcement, Iran lost its largest commercial partner in the Gulf and the principal channel through which the bloc has moved goods and money around sanctions for two decades.
This is the real risk. The pact is more dangerous than its text implies. The two overland routes Iran still has are controlled by states now tied to Riyadh by mutual defence obligations. They do not need to use force. Slower customs, tighter banking, or a closed border would do more harm than any defence clause. Iran cannot respond to a NATO member and a nuclear-armed neighbour as it does to American bases in the Gulf.
This is where the ruling bloc’s strategy is most exposed. Its wager is that Iran returns to negotiations holding Hormuz and converts that leverage into investment and sanctions relief. Ghalibaf has reiterated that the strait will remain closed until Washington lifts its blockade and releases Iran’s frozen assets. But Trump now says there are no talks under way, and everything meant to follow a deal requires neighbours willing to trade with Iran.
For now, downplaying the Mecca pact serves its purpose. It steadies Iran’s negotiators and protects the economic programme that underpins the bloc’s authority. But this is composure, not analysis. A bloc organised for war can judge military threats but is less able to see dangers that do not take military form. Iran is not being encircled. It is being excluded from the arrangements its neighbours are making, and its own actions are speeding up that process. If this continues, the reckoning will come not on the battlefield but in the accounts.
Kayhan Valadbaygi is a Research Fellow at the International Institute of Social History (IISH) in Amsterdam and CEO of Middle East Risk & Reform Advisory.
Have questions or comments? Email us at: editorial-english@alaraby.co.uk
