articles.title: Russia capable of producing over 200 ballistic, cruise missiles monthly – Defense Intelligence
articles.body:
According to the Main Intelligence Agency (GUR) of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, Russia currently possesses over 600 Oniks missiles, reports Ukrainska Pravda, citing a GUR response to an inquiry.
In addition to the Oniks missiles, the Russian army also has 450 Kalibrs, over 120 Zircons, about 130 missiles for Iskander-M systems, 400 RM-48U missiles for S-400 systems, and up to 100 Kh-101 missiles.
At the same time, as of July, Russia had about 50 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles and approximately the same number of North Korean ballistic missiles (KN-23, KN-24, and KN-30).
"The main focus of Russia’s defense-industrial complex is shifting toward mass missile systems. Priority in production is given to missiles for the Iskander-M complex, as well as Kh-101 and Kalibr missiles. Russia maintains high production rates and, in certain cases, exceeds planned indicators," GUR emphasized.
Thus, according to current estimates, the military-industrial complex of the aggressor state is capable of producing over two hundred cruise and ballistic missiles of various types each month.
Currently, the planned monthly production target for 9M723 missiles for Iskander-M systems is 60 units. In July, the Russian military-industrial complex exceeded this figure, manufacturing 65 such missiles.
Additionally, in July, Russia produced 87 Kh-101 cruise missiles.
Production rates for RM-48U missiles for S-400 systems are estimated at approximately 50 units per month. In total throughout 2026, Russia plans to manufacture over 480 such missiles—more than double the plan set for 2025.

articles.title: Pentagon seeks contractor for HAWK missile system sustainment
articles.body:
- The U.S. Army issued a Sources Sought notice for HAWK missile system sustainment support, with responses due September 2, 2026.
- The contract would cover logistics, engineering and maintenance for HAWK systems used by Foreign Military Sales and partner nations, including Ukraine.
U.S. Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal has issued a request for information seeking contractors capable of providing total system sustainment for the HAWK missile system, according to a Sources Sought notice.
The Army said it is not committed to issuing a solicitation or awarding a contract as a result of the announcement. Responses are due September 2 at 1:00 p.m. EST.
The work covers the Fair Share Sustainment Operations program and Contract Logistics Services for the HAWK system, officially known as the Homing All the Way Killer. The Army wants a contractor to take on total system performance responsibility, covering logistics, engineering services, material supply, test support, product assurance, configuration management and technical documentation. The scope also includes integration support for Sentinel, NASAMS and short-range air defense systems.
The contractor would support fielded Foreign Military Sales and Building Partner Capacity nations operating HAWK ground support equipment and missiles. Work would center on White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico, including Launch Complex 32’s HAWK Support Center and the Theater Readiness Monitoring Facility, a government-owned, contractor-operated site that houses a HAWK ground support equipment test bed, as well as fielded Theater Readiness Monitoring Facilities and Certified Round Assembly Facilities operated by partner nations.
Interested firms must submit a statement of qualifications by the response deadline. The Army’s notice specifies exactly what that submission needs to include: the firm’s name and address, its Unique Entity ID and CAGE Code, a point of contact with phone number and email, the company’s business size status including any service-disabled veteran-owned designation, and a summary of the firm’s expertise providing logistics services for HAWK systems. Companies must also cite relevant past contracts, including scope, quantities delivered, contract numbers and a point of contact who can verify performance.
The draft Performance Work Statement itself contains Controlled Unclassified Information and is not included in the public notice. Companies must formally request it from the contracting officer and include a brief qualifications narrative for the HAWK system before the Army will consider releasing it.
HAWK is a decades-old medium-range air defense system that the U.S. military first fielded in the 1960s. The Army has continued sustaining it for allied and partner nations that still operate the system through the Foreign Military Sales program, even though the system was retired from U.S. Army service years ago.
Ukraine received its first MIM-23 HAWK batteries in late 2022 and early 2023. Spain transferred several batteries, and the United States supplied refurbished missiles; other partner nations later contributed additional components. Ukrainian crews trained on the system quickly, according to the country’s Air Force.
Ukraine’s Air Force has reported that HAWK batteries have intercepted Kh-59 cruise missiles, Kalibr cruise missiles and Shahed-type attack drones, including one case in which a single launcher downed three cruise missiles in succession. Ukrainian operators have described the system as reliable and workable even at night, according to the Air Force’s public statements. Ukraine’s use of the system between 2023 and 2026 has shown that the roughly 60-year-old design can still perform against modern threats when integrated properly into a broader air defense network.

articles.title: The Fedorov protesters lost. But they backed a man for what he built, not what he promised—and that may be new in Ukraine.
articles.body:
On 19 August, veteran and civic activist Dmytro Koziatynskyi thanked everyone who had taken part in the month-long protests to bring back Mykhailo Fedorov, and said it was all worth it. Koziatynskyi was one of the organizers of rallies across Ukrainian cities demanding the reinstatement of Fedorov, the defense minister widely credited with driving Ukraine's military-tech overhaul, after he was abruptly dismissed on 14 July.
His firing detonated a month of protests because Fedorov was no ordinary minister: the 35-year-old reformer had exposed billions in defense overspending and built the drone programs many Ukrainians saw as their best chance in the war, so his removal read, to those in the streets, as the old system protecting itself.
Koziatynskyi's decision to end his protest came after Parliament voted 312 that same day to appoint Yevhenii Khmara as defense minister. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy did not meet the protesters' main demand: the return of Fedorov.
"It is a pity that we were never able to establish a dialogue between the authorities and society. I hope this issue will be resolved over time because, in my view, the lack of communication was the root cause of these protests," Koziatynskyi writes.
Ukraine’s cardboard protests look like democracy working. In a war, that’s also the risk.
But the rallies may leave Ukrainian society with something that outlasts the outcome of one personnel decision, Anatolii Romaniuk, a political scientist at Ivan Franko National University in Lviv, told Euromaidan Press. The protesters lost: Parliament appointed Yevhenii Khmara as defense minister, not Mykhailo Fedorov. Yet the "cardboard Maidan," as the protests were termed for their abundance of handmade signs, may have revealed the beginnings of a broader shift in Ukrainian society. Romaniuk believes its significance lies in why people took to the streets: to support a politician not because of what he promised them, but because of what he had already done.
Actions, not words
Romaniuk believes Ukrainian society has long lived under what he calls a "political curse": large numbers of Ukrainians repeatedly bought into populist promises from politicians offering things that were simply unrealistic.
He points to every Ukrainian election from 2004 through 2019, arguing that the share of populist promises only increased. Experts could see that many of them were impossible to fulfill, he says, yet voters continued to support politicians who made them. Romaniuk points to a promise from the 2019 election campaign that Ukrainian wages would overtake Poland's—at a time when the average salary in Ukraine was around $400 a month, and Poland's was roughly three times that.
The 2026 protests may represent a change in perspective, he argues: people backed a politician not for what he said he would do, but for what he had already done.
Fedorov's signature result was an audit—in his first months, his ministry exposed roughly $7.2 billion (300 billion hryvnia) in defense overspending, and that figure became the movement's rallying cry. "The audit showed 300 billion in theft. They removed the auditor, not the thieves," read one cardboard sign in Lviv.
“They removed the auditor, not the thieves”: why Ukrainians are protesting Zelenskyy’s reshuffle
The protesters were defending a record: open procurement built on the Brave1 marketplace, where frontline units order drones directly from certified manufacturers; a first competitive tender that cut 155mm shell prices by 16%; and, above all, Fedorov's bet on robotization—technology instead of manpower—that many Ukrainians saw as their best chance against a larger Russian army, a way to spend drones rather than lives. Fedorov was removed while he was implementing the reform, amid a conflict with then Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi.
"If this change in perspective continues, we will get out of the situation where we have become hostages to a growing wave of populism that would otherwise simply overwhelm us in the next elections. Because the degree, or the level, of populism in the 2019 elections was already very high. It was unrealistic," Romaniuk says of the protests' possible longer-term effect.
The protesters were "for," not "against"
Romaniuk sees another distinction between these demonstrations and earlier protests in Ukraine's modern history: previous movements were built around being "against" something. This time, the demand was explicitly "for" something.
"If we recall the events of the 2014 Euromaidan Revolution, and even last year's protests, they were 'against.' That is, they were against Yanukovych signing an agreement with Russia and refusing to sign the Association Agreement. They were against a decision made at the highest level in Ukraine to restrict the anti-corruption bodies," Romaniuk says, referring to former President Viktor Yanukovych, whose 2013 pivot away from the European Union set off the Euromaidan Revolution.
He argues that Ukraine has never before seen protests explicitly organized in support of a government official, making the Fedorov rallies a first.
At the same time, Romaniuk acknowledges the paradox: even protests framed as being "against" something almost always implied support for an alternative. In 2004, for example, Ukrainians protested the results of the second round of a falsified presidential election that had declared pro-Russian Viktor Yanukovych the winner over his pro-European rival, Viktor Yushchenko. But by opposing those results, Romaniuk says, they were also supporting democratic elections.
Ukraine’s ousted defense minister took drone contracts away from the generals. Now they may take them back
The difference this time is that the "for" was clearly articulated. Protesters demanding Fedorov's return had an idea of the kind of Ukraine they wanted to see.
"In these protests, we have a situation where people are supporting the course pursued by Defense Minister Fedorov—the modernization of the army, changing approaches to warfare, and changing what the Ukrainian state should look like," Romaniuk says.
Dariia, a 22-year-old who attended the protests in Lviv, describes her reasons for joining them in similar terms.
"My motivation is to see changes in the country, to see justice, to see that young, progressive people who put technology ahead of human losses are leading us toward victory."
She says Fedorov was one of the people introducing reforms "from the very top of government all the way to the battlefield."
"And we really saw those changes," Dariia told Euromaidan Press. She credits Fedorov with the long-range drone campaign that has struck Russian refineries, defense plants, and Wildberries depots as far as Bashkortostan, some 1,300 kilometers inside Russia: "Our enemy finds ways to attack, and we must also search for new ways to respond. Fedorov, as defense minister, was the person finding ways to respond to these attacks, how to carry out deep strikes."
Ukraine’s defense minister explained how the country buys weapons—after he was sacked
This year's cardboard protests could be a good start
Romaniuk cautions that it is still too early to speak of a change in Ukrainians' political culture. But he says he would like to see this episode become the beginning of one.
"I would like other people in power to also be judged by their results, by what they have done," he says.
A genuine pattern, he adds, could only be established if similar cases repeated themselves. For now, this remains one specific episode rather than a proven trend.
Dariia connects the rallies to her own experience of protesting more than a decade earlier.
"I remember the rallies in Mykolaiv in 2014 against the occupation regime in the east. Back then, it was five people with cardboard signs standing in the rain. My family was one of them. Nobody came out, nobody understood that position… It is nice to see that people in the south and east understand now," Dariia says.

articles.title: North Korea fires 10 missiles day after Trump curtails South Korea joint drills
articles.body:
North Korea has launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea, South Korea’s military said, a day after Pyongyang shrugged off Donald Trump’s order to scale back US military drills with South Korea in an apparent attempt to resume diplomacy.
The joint chiefs of staff said the missiles were launched from the region of Pyongyang at around 5pm (08.00 GMT) on Thursday towards North Korea’s eastern waters.
The military said South Korea had bolstered its surveillance and was closely coordinating information on the launches with the US and Japan.
South Korea’s presidential national security council held an emergency meeting, after which it issued a statement urging North Korea to halt ballistic missile launches, which are banned under UN security council resolutions.
The Japanese prime minister’s office said earlier that it had detected a suspected missile launch.
On Wednesday, the South Korean and US militaries said they were scaling back their 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises. Donald Trump had ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the exercises just before they began on Monday. Explaining his reasons for the decision, the US president cited what he said was a good relationship with North Korea’s leader, Kim Jong-un, and South Korea’s refusal to support him over the war against Iran.
Kim Yo-jong, the influential sister of the North Korean leader, dismissed Trump’s overture on Wednesday, saying it was not worthy of comment.
“The provocative, aggressive nature of the drills won’t change even though their duration and size were reduced,” she said. “If the US calculates that it can propagate its recent measure as one of so-called good faith, they will not get the desired answer.”
She highlighted a series of other military drills carried out by the US and South Korea earlier this year and South Korea’s push to introduce nuclear-powered submarines.
However, Kim Yo-jong refrained from the typical North Korean reaction of fiery rhetoric, and said personal relations between her brother and Trump were “still excellent”. That could signal a desire by Pyongyang to wait for Trump to make bigger concessions before returning to talks.
She denied Trump’s claim that Kim Jong-un had responded to his request for a conversation.
When asked by reporters on Wednesday if he would be meeting Kim Jong-un this year, Trump said: “Yeah, I will be.” He would not answer a question about whether he was exchanging letters with Kim, but said he got along with him.

articles.title: NATO says ready as Iran reportedly considers European targets
articles.body:
Iran has examined possible strikes on military targets in southeastern Europe if U.S. President Donald Trump expands military operations against Tehran, the Financial Times reported, citing two people close to the Iranian government.
Iranian forces have assessed U.S. assets in Bulgaria, where parliament last month approved the temporary deployment of American aerial refueling aircraft at Bezmer Air Base, according to the report.
Bulgaria authorized up to eight U.S. KC-135 tanker aircraft and 250 military personnel to use the base from July 24 to Oct. 1 in support of American operations in the Middle East.
One of the sources also named the island of Cyprus as a possible target in the event of a renewed U.S. offensive.
A British air base on the island was struck by a drone in March.
The report presented the options as contingency planning and gave no indication that an attack had been ordered.
Responding to the report, a NATO official said the alliance was prepared for any threat and described its deterrence and defense posture as “strong and effective.”
The official pointed to four occasions earlier this year when NATO air-defense systems intercepted ballistic missiles launched from Iran toward Türkiye.
Greece, meanwhile, is considering moving a Patriot air-defense battery from the southeastern Aegean island of Karpathos to the Souda naval base on Crete, Kathimerini reported.
The transfer would be considered if Souda were assessed to face a significant threat, Greek defense sources told the newspaper. Souda Bay hosts a major Greek and NATO military facility.

articles.title: Russia and Ukraine are sending assault groups deep behind enemy lines, blurring the front line
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine are sending assault groups deep behind enemy lines, blurring the front line
The nature of the war has changed once again. Not only in the rear, where the intensity of mutual strikes has increased and warehouses belonging to online marketplaces and other businesses have often become targets. There have also been changes at the front, in tactics. Traditional infiltration by small groups has reached a new level. Now assault units try to slip through undetected not for hundreds of meters, but for kilometers. Sometimes the depth of these raids exceeds 10 kilometers. The idea is that such groups do not require large amounts of supplies and can therefore operate cut off from the main forces. The raids destabilize the enemy’s defenses and can also be dangerous for its drone operators. This has created a new picture at the front: in many sectors, the battle formations of the two armies have become intermixed; control over roads and towns is often unstable; villages change hands several times a week.
Kramatorsk agglomeration
- Russian forces are pressing their offensive on Kramatorsk and Sloviansk from several directions. Having captured most of Kostiantynivka — where video-documented resistance from Ukrainian troops has all but disappeared, suggesting most remaining Ukrainian forces there have withdrawn or been killed — Russian units are now trying to launch an assault on the next settlement along the road to Kramatorsk, the village of Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka. Fighting continues on the village’s southern outskirts, but Russian forces have failed to significantly improve their position there over the past two weeks. The main Russian force in the area is likely still busy clearing Kostiantynivka and nearby villages.
- East of Kostiantynivka, Russian forces have opened a path into the rear of Ukrainian troops that have held positions near Chasiv Yar for years, forcing a Ukrainian retreat in this sector along the Siverskyi Donets–Donbas Canal.
- Farther north along the canal, Russian forces are trying to expand a foothold just outside Kramatorsk, where assault units advanced several kilometers in quick succession and captured Vasyutynske, 5 to 7 kilometers (3 to 4 miles) from the city. Progress in this sector has slowed in recent weeks, since Ukrainian positions remain “intermixed” with Russian ones along the canal’s banks.
- Northwest of Kostiantynivka, Russian troops continue advancing along the Kazenyi Torets River toward Druzhkivka, pushing into the rear of the Ukrainian group defending the Kostiantynivka area. In recent weeks, they have captured Krasnyi Kut and reached Raiske, just 3 to 5 kilometers (2 to 3 miles) from Druzhkivka’s southwestern outskirts.
- Farther west, a Russian group fighting its way toward Dobropillia — the largest settlement in northwestern Donetsk region — has spent months battling to capture villages and towns on the city’s southern approaches, including Shevchenko, Chernihivske, and Krasnopodillia. That raises the threat that an assault on Dobropillia itself could begin soon. Russia’s Defense Ministry claims such an assault is already underway, carried out by troops it says infiltrated from the direction of Novyi Donbas, but that claim remains unconfirmed.
Where the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Dnipro regions meet
- Along the front stretching from Orikhiv, in central Zaporizhzhia region, to the point where the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Dnipro regions meet — where Ukrainian and Russian offensives are underway simultaneously — the trend toward deep raids is especially pronounced. The terrain helps explain why: steppe broken up by tree lines, rivers, ravines, and small, scattered settlements. In places, the fighting resembles maneuver warfare, with small groups of troops moving by vehicle and trying to “catch” similarly small enemy units, though more often assault troops move on foot through the steppe and tree lines.
- Drones are the main defense against these raids in areas thinly held by infantry. Fragmentary reports suggest drone operators themselves have sometimes become targets of enemy assault troops who infiltrated the area.
- Adding to the confusion, commanders on both sides are trying to demonstrate superiority through so-called “flag-planting” campaigns, ordering assault troops to prove their presence in various settlements by literally planting a flag there.
- Two large such campaigns played out on August 12 and 13. Ukrainian forces first raised flags in several villages across two sectors: in the Russian rear along the Haichur River (Rybne, Krasnohirske, Zlahoda, and Pryvilne), and farther east, where Ukrainian troops are trying to break through at the junction of the Russian Tsentr and Vostok groups in the Mokri Yaly valley (Yalta, Novokhatske, Tolstoi, Zelenyi Hai, and Piddubne). A day later, Russian forces raised their own flags in most of the same villages — sometimes no more than 100 meters (330 feet) from where the Ukrainian flags had gone up.
- The two sides’ explanations for the incidents naturally diverge, generally boiling down to accusations that the enemy published old footage, generated it with AI, or sent soldiers on one-way suicide missions purely for political effect. Russia’s version has an inherent advantage, since videos of Russian flags surfaced later — disproving it would require assuming Russian commanders knew in advance where Ukrainian forces planned to “plant their flags” and had prepared rebuttals ahead of time. Either way, it is currently impossible to reliably determine who controls specific settlements.
- The Ukrainian offensives on the northern flank, in the Haichur and Mokri Yaly valleys, were aimed at slowing the Russian advance eastward from Huliaipole toward Orikhiv — and largely succeeded. The main forces of the Russian Vostok group stalled for several months on their approach to Orikhiv, forcing Russian commanders to send reserves to counter Ukrainian brigades advancing from the north. Now the Russian advance has resumed thanks to a new tactic: assault units from the area of Vozdvyzhenka, a village that has changed hands several times, slipped through the steppe to reach the T0480 highway leading north from Orikhiv, near Liubytske and Novosoloshyne.
- At the same time, forces from Russia’s 58th Combined Arms Army, part of the Dnepr group, took advantage of the Vostok group’s advance to step up their own offensive on Orikhiv from the south. Russian assault units broke through what had once been an impenetrable Ukrainian defense at Novodanylivka, reached the southern outskirts of Orikhiv, and seized a stretch of the Orikhiv–Mala Tokmachka road.
- Russian wa bloggers reported that Russian forces had once again captured Mala Tokmachka — a town that has become something of a running joke — but it remains unconfirmed.
Kharkiv region
- Russian forces opened several new incursions of varying size along the entire Russia–Kharkiv region border in 2025 and 2026, but the two main fronts remain the older, interconnected footholds near Vovchansk and Kupiansk. Russian commanders had planned as early as 2024 to capture both district centers and push deeper into Kharkiv region toward Velykyi Burluk and Izyum, with the ultimate goal of cutting off the Ukrainian-controlled part of Donbas from the rest of the region.
- The Russian army did not capture the ruins of Vovchansk until early 2026 and still has not fully occupied Kupiansk. Ukrainian forces not only halted the Russian advance there but recaptured the southern part of the city and most of its center in a late-2025 offensive.
- After regrouping, Russian forces again went on the offensive against the city center, Zaoskillia — the half of Kupiansk on the Oskil River’s eastern bank — and neighboring industrial towns. By the end of summer, Russian forces had reached the river’s eastern bank in several places and once again seized central districts on the western bank, though Ukrainian forces continue to hold back the advance around the city.
- Near Vovchansk, however, the redeployment of Ukrainian troops to Kupiansk for the winter offensive weakened the defense there, allowing Russian forces to infiltrate the front line with relatively large units from two directions — from the north, out of occupied Vovchansk, and from the east, across the border at the village of Artelne.
- The groups that infiltrated from Vovchansk reached the outskirts of Bilyi Kolodiaz, but Ukrainian forces pushed them back. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its forces had captured the village, which is important for supplying the Ukrainian group, and videos later surfaced showing Russian assault units massing in tree lines to the north.
- Capturing Bilyi Kolodiaz and the surrounding area would open the way for Russian forces to break through to Velykyi Burluk, in the rear of the Ukrainian group defending Kupiansk.

articles.title: Japan ‘playing with fire’ over nuclear ambitions – China
articles.body:
Japan ‘playing with fire’ over nuclear ambitions – China
Russia and China are both opposed to Japan’s accelerating militarization and growing debate over acquiring nuclear weapons, Beijing’s ambassador to Moscow, Zhang Hanhui, has said, warning that Tokyo’s policies could trigger a new arms race.
In an article published by TASS on Thursday, Zhang said Moscow and Beijing had reached a “high degree of consensus” over Japan. “Beijing and Moscow consider it necessary to remain highly vigilant and firmly oppose Japan’s accelerated remilitarization and its pursuit of nuclear weapons,” he wrote.
The envoy warned that if Tokyo decides to create its own nuclear weapons, the strategic balance in Northeast Asia will be completely disrupted, and “a nuclear arms race in the region could erupt at any moment”. “If Japan’s right-wing forces continue to play with fire on nuclear policy, the Japanese will ultimately once again find themselves in the dock of history,” Zhang added.
The warning comes after, in December 2025, a senior official involved in devising Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s security policy reportedly argued that Japan should consider acquiring nuclear weapons as the US nuclear umbrella is becoming increasingly unreliable. “In the end, we can only rely on ourselves,” the official was quoted as saying.
Publicly, Takaichi has stressed that Japan still adheres to three non-nuclear principles – a long-time policy stating that Tokyo will not possess, produce or permit the introduction of nuclear weapons.
However, she has questioned the latter principle, while Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has argued that “one topic we cannot avoid is nuclear weapons,” adding that the issue should be discussed “without any taboos.”
In this vein, Zhang accused the Japanese leadership of hiding nuclear ambitions behind the country’s status as the only nation to have suffered atomic bombings in war, saying Japanese leadership had begun “dangerous experiments in nuclear policy” while trying to revive “the spirit of militarism.”
The envoy also alluded to Japan’s nuclear prowess, recalling that the country possesses about 44.4 tons of separated civilian plutonium. “This amount is sufficient for the production of approximately 5,500 nuclear warheads,” he said. “Given the desire and appropriate capabilities, Japan becoming a nuclear power no longer looks like fantasy.”
Russia has voiced similar concerns. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has called debate over revising Japan’s non-nuclear principles a “serious signal,” while Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko warned that abandoning the policy would worsen security in Northeast Asia.

articles.title: Trump threatens states trading with Iran in new 'economic war'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump threatens countries trading with Iran in new 'economic war'
US President Donald Trump has announced an "unprecedented" economic campaign against Iran, threatening severe penalties against countries and companies that continue to provide Tehran with financial or commercial support.
Trump said in a post on Truth Social that Iran had failed to seize opportunities to reach an agreement with Washington and declared "the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country".
"No one has given the Islamic Republic of Iran a greater opportunity to make a Deal than me. TRAGICALLY, for them, they have failed to take it." Trump wrote.
"Therefore, today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY! This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale," he added, claiming that Iran's navy had been eliminated, its air force destroyed, its military factories reduced to rubble and its currency rendered worthless.
Trump threatened countries that allow their financial institutions, businesses, airports or government bodies to provide a "lifeline" to Iran, warning that they would face "TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences".
He also called for an immediate halt to "oil smuggling", barter arrangements, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries and front companies linked to Iran.
"It all needs to stop NOW," Trump said, calling on US allies to join Washington in isolating Tehran.
He said the measures would cripple Iran's ability to operate and reiterated that Washington would not allow Tehran to obtain a nuclear weapon.
"IRAN WILL NEVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON," he wrote.
Trump's announcement provided no details on what new measures Washington would impose or which countries could be targeted.
His comments suggested the US could expand the use of secondary sanctions against countries and companies dealing with Iran, potentially increasing pressure on some of Tehran's largest trading partners.
The announcement comes amid a broader US shift towards economic pressure on Iran following months of military confrontation.
Trump plays down Hormuz
Earlier on Wednesday, Trump said he believed the Strait of Hormuz would become less important to energy markets because of growing US oil production and the construction of new pipelines.
"We're taking out a lot of oil," Trump told reporters during a meeting with technology executives at the White House.
He pointed to production in Texas, Louisiana and elsewhere, saying new energy infrastructure was reducing reliance on the strategic waterway.
"I think the Strait of Hormuz will not be nearly as important as it was in the past," he said.
Trump also claimed that the US blockade on Iran had been "100 percent" successful and said restrictions on Iranian ports would continue in an effort to prevent ships from entering or leaving Iran while allowing other vessels to pass.
He predicted that oil prices would continue to fall sharply.
Despite the intensified pressure, Trump left open the possibility that negotiations with Tehran could resume.
"Maybe at some point, but I think we're in a good position right now," he said when asked when talks might restart.
Trump said several oil tankers were continuing to pass through the Strait of Hormuz carrying large quantities of crude.
"We have complete control of the Strait of Hormuz, except for some annoying things from time to time, like them shooting down a drone," he said.
On Iran's nuclear programme, Trump repeated that Tehran must completely abandon any attempt to acquire nuclear weapons.
"They have to get rid of it completely," he said. "Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon."
Secret Hormuz shipping corridor
Axios reported on Wednesday, citing US officials, that the US military had established a secret maritime corridor through the Strait of Hormuz to facilitate the movement of millions of barrels of oil each day.
The report said between 15 and 20 oil tankers had entered and exited the strait through a southern route along the coast of Oman as part of an operation running for several weeks.
Trump on Tuesday again spoke of declaring the Strait of Hormuz "American territory", posting a map on Truth Social showing the waterway circled alongside the words "New American Territory".
In a later post, Trump said there were "no talks or discussions underway, or scheduled, with Iran" and that the naval blockade remained fully in force.
He also said the Strait of Hormuz remained "open and operational" and claimed that all sea mines had either been removed or destroyed.

Russia May Have Lost Two Key Kalibr Missile Carriers in Novorossiysk Strike
Two Russian Black Sea Fleet frigates, Admiral Makarov and Admiral Essen, reportedly sustained serious damage during an August 12 strike on the Novorossiysk naval base, according to Militarnyi on August 20, citing an analysis by the OSINT account Absolutely Reliable Source.
Satellite imagery released by the account appears to show damage to the frigates’ missile launch systems, raising the possibility that both vessels may have lost their ability to launch Kalibr cruise missiles. The exact extent of the damage has not been officially disclosed.

The frigate’s Trebovaniye-M combat information and control system was also damaged.
Admiral Makarov, the flagship of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, was reportedly struck in the area of its vertical launch systems. According to the analysis, the impact caused an internal detonation and burned out the ship’s 3S14 launch cells.
The frigate also sustained damage to its radar, electronic warfare, and communications systems.
If the reported damage is confirmed, Russia’s Black Sea Fleet may have lost the operational use of two of its principal Kalibr missile carriers, the outlet reported.
Both vessels could also require extensive repairs if the damage to their launch systems is confirmed, with their return to combat service potentially taking at least a year, according to the assessment.
On August 12, Ukrainian forces launched an overnight strike against Russia’s naval base in Novorossiysk, targeting air defense positions, port berths, and other naval infrastructure, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Zelenskyy described the operation as unique, noting that Novorossiysk serves as Russia’s last major naval stronghold in the Black Sea and lies more than 300 kilometers from the frontline.

articles.title: Until Ukraine has sufficient anti-ballistic defenses, Moscow will not seriously consider peace — Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Until Ukraine has sufficient anti-ballistic defenses, Moscow will not seriously consider peace — Zelenskyy
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy said that Ukraine needs Patriot interceptor missiles every day. The Freyja anti-ballistic shield is undergoing integration and testing.
Russia will not seriously consider peace until Ukraine has enough missiles to shoot down ballistic missiles. While the Freyja antiballistic shield project is still under development, Ukraine needs missiles for American Patriot air defense systems. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this, UNN writes.
"Unfortunately, while Moscow is investing in ballistic missiles and escalation, the world does not always respond appropriately to such strikes. And as long as Ukraine has insufficient antiballistic capabilities, Russia will not seriously consider peace. We are doing everything to ensure protection, and work on the Freyja program is ongoing every day," Zelenskyy reported.
According to him, American interceptors for Patriot air defense systems cannot yet be replaced, and Ukraine needs them every day.
"Every additional missile saves the lives of our people. I thank everyone who understands this and seeks and finds opportunities to help," the head of state emphasized
It should be added
Fire Point CEO and CTO Iryna Terekh said during the DALO Industry Days arms exhibition, which is taking place in Denmark, that Freyja is currently at the stage of integrating all components into a single system and conducting tests.
"Right now, we have begun the most interesting part of Freyja's development from an engineering standpoint—technical integration of the entire ecosystem, together with the radars, the launcher, the data transmission channel, and the command center," she said.
According to her, tests are conducted up to twice a week, after which adjustments are made to the system.
The project to create a joint European antiballistic shield, Freyja, officially began on July 13, when Ukraine and nine other European countries signed the declaration of the Antiballistic Coalition. At that time, 12 defense companies joined it, including HENSOLDT, Thales, Diehl Defence, Saab, Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace, Weibel, Leonardo, MBDA, Eurosam, Safran, and Destinus.
The Freyja project, which is intended to provide interception of Russian ballistic missiles, is being built around the FP-7.x interceptor missile developed by Fire Point; other system components are being provided by European defense companies.
As reported by UNN, according to Fire Point co-founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman, the involvement of European governments, including the German government, has significantly accelerated the implementation of Freyja. Provided that bureaucratic procedures in the partner countries move quickly, the first FP-7.X interceptor missiles could be ready by the end of 2026. Fire Point plans to carry out the first interception of a ballistic target by the Freyja system by the end of 2027.
At the beginning of August, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that new partners were planning to join Freyja.

articles.title: Belgium lines up a “drone deal” to tap Ukraine’s war-tested know-how
articles.body:
Ukraine and Belgium are drawing up a bilateral agreement to deepen cooperation on drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after meeting Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot in Kyiv on 18 August. The two also discussed strengthening Ukraine's air power and shielding it from Russian attacks.
Cheap drones now decide much of the fighting, and Kyiv has turned years of learning to fly and defeat them into leverage—trading that edge for weapons and money with a lengthening line of Western partners.
A new deal takes shape
Teams on both sides are now writing the text of the Drone Deal and weighing possible dates to sign it, ArmyInform reported. Ukraine is ready to share its own expertise in unmanned systems with partners, Zelenskyy said.
Defense ran through the meeting, with both sides focused on strengthening Ukraine's combat aviation and defending its skies.
"I expect that we will be able to implement what we discussed, and there will be more protection from Russian strikes," Zelenskyy said.
Belgium has promised 30 F-16 fighter jets—the largest F-16 pledge from any single country—though none have reached Ukraine yet, with deliveries tied to Belgium's own switch to newer aircraft.
Belgium's deeper backing
Zelenskyy thanked Belgium for more than $1.28 billion in support this year, covering defense and civilian needs alike, and for backing Ukraine's move toward the European Union. The military share flows from a standing pledge: since 2025, Belgium has committed to at least $1.16 billion in defense aid a year.
A 2024 security pact locked in that relationship, making a small Western European country one of Ukraine's steadier partners. Belgian firms also service the F-16s Ukraine already flies, the jets delivered by other partners in the coalition.

articles.title: Russia attacks Ukraine with various missiles and 168 drones, Kyiv Oblast was the main target
articles.body:
Russia attacks Ukraine with various missiles and 168 drones, Kyiv Oblast was the main target
Russia launched a large-scale attack on Ukraine on the night of 19-20 August using various types of missiles and 168 drones. Kyiv Oblast was the main target of the attack. Ukrainian air defences have downed 186 aerial assets.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Details: According to the Air Force, starting from 18:00 on 19 August, Russian forces attacked Kyiv Oblast with Oniks, Zircon and Iskander-M missiles and missiles fired from S-400 systems that approach their targets on a ballistic trajectory.
They were launched from Russia's Kursk, Rostov and Bryansk oblasts.
Another 36 Kh-101, Iskander-K and Kh-59 cruise and air-launched missiles were launched from the airspace over Russia's Vologda, Kursk and Belgorod oblasts.
Eight Kalibr cruise missiles were launched from the area of the city of Novorossiysk. Russian forces also used two Banderol loitering munitions.
In addition, Russia attacked Ukraine with 168 Shahed and Gerbera attack drones and Parodiya decoy drones. Almost half of the Shahed UAVs launched were jet-powered.
The drones were launched from the areas of Kursk, Millerovo, Oryol and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea.
The Air Force stressed that Kyiv Oblast was the main target of the Russian attack.
The aerial attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from the defence forces.
Quote: "As of 09:30, air defence had shot down/jammed 31 Kh-101/Iskander-K/Kh-59 cruise missiles, eight Kalibr cruise missiles, two Banderol loitering munitions and 145 enemy Shahed and Gerbera-type UAVs and drones of other types in the north, south, east and centre of the country.
Hits by enemy aerial weapons were recorded at 28 locations, and debris from downed weapons landed at 2 locations."
Background:
- On the night of 19-20 August, Russian forces attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles, with explosions heard in the city. A building and a children's hospital were damaged, and fires broke out.
- So far, 12 people are known to have been killed and 34 injured.
- On the night of 19-20 August, the Russian military launched a combined attack on Kyiv Oblast using drones, ballistic missiles and cruise missiles, killing one person and injuring seven others.

articles.title: Romania destroys a sea drone and finds aerial drone debris on its soil amid Russia’s attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
Romania destroyed an explosives-laden maritime drone near its critical Neptun Deep gas platform and recovered debris from a separate aerial drone that crashed on its soil, the Romanian Defense Ministry reported. The incidents came during a major Russian attack on Ukraine on 20 August that killed 14 people in Kyiv city and oblast, caused incidents in Moldova, and triggered air defense activation in Poland.
F-16 fires cannon at sea drone near gas platform
A commercial vessel spotted a drifting maritime drone near the Neptun Alpha production platform, approximately 80 nautical miles east of Constanța, at around 06:28, the Defense Ministry said. Two Romanian F-16s scrambled with orders to fire. One engaged the target with its onboard cannon—the first time Romania used a cannon against a drone and the first engagement against a maritime drone. All previous shootdowns used air-to-air missiles against aerial drones.
The country's Defense Minister Radu Miruță said the drone was carrying explosives and was spotted just hundreds of meters from the platform where several hundred people work. Through a recently established direct communication channel, Ukraine confirmed the drone was not of Ukrainian origin. President Nicușor Dan directly blamed Russia, condemning "the intensification of these types of irresponsible incidents on the part of the Russian Federation."
The engagement came nine days after Romanian navy divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones drifting near the same platform by controlled detonation.
14 killed as Russia unleashes massive overnight barrage on unprotected Kyiv, striking homes, hospital, school and railway infrastructure
Aerial drone crashes in Romania's Tulcea County
Earlier overnight, Romanian radar detected aerial targets near the Ukrainian border at 02:23, the Defense Ministry said. Two Spanish F-18s from NATO's air policing mission and a Romanian IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter scrambled. At 03:21, a drone crossed into Romanian airspace 13 km east of Galați and crashed three minutes later near the village of Grindu in Tulcea County. No casualties or damage were reported. The fragments posed no explosive hazard.
The crash came four days after a Spanish F-18 shot down another drone over Romanian airspace, Euronews reported. Romanian F-16s intercepted three Russian drones in July.
Russian Shaheds hit near Moldova-border crossing, burn food cargo, and black out 13,000 in Odesa Oblast
Poland activates defenses, Moldova hit by drone spillover
Poland's Operational Command activated military aircraft and ground-based air defense systems during the Russian attack as a preventive measure. The Netherlands provided air defense support. No breach of Polish airspace was recorded.
Moldova faced multiple incidents. At 03:16, the country's National Army detected what was preliminarily identified as a Shahed-136/Geran-2 drone crossing from Ukraine near Kotlovyna in Odesa Oblast into Moldova's Gagauzia region. It returned to Ukrainian airspace six minutes later, public broadcaster Moldova1 said.
Separately, an explosion at a truck parking lot on Ukrainian territory about 150 meters from the Giurgiulești-Reni border crossing at around 03:45 sparked a fire that spread onto Moldovan soil, Newsmaker reported. Border police found drone fragments in a crater approximately 1 km inside Moldovan territory.

articles.title: "Darkness, night, everything on fire": Kyiv residents speak about Russia's latest attack on Kyiv
articles.body:
"Darkness, night, everything on fire": Kyiv residents speak about Russia's latest attack on Kyiv
Fifteen people were killed and 39 injured as a result of a Russian attack on Kyiv on the night of 19-20 August. Residents of damaged buildings have shared how they survived the night.
Source: Ukrainian public broadcasters Suspilne and Radio Liberty
Details: A multi-storey residential building in the Solomianskyi district of Kyiv was damaged. The State Emergency Service is conducting search and rescue operations there.
Larysa, a resident of the destroyed building, told Suspilne that the explosions occurred shortly before midnight. Larysa lived on the fifth floor and the collapse occurred at the level of the seventh and eighth floors.
"It was very loud, it has never been this loud here. The last loud strike was the missile that hit the building. It caught fire, there was a blaze and destruction, and windows were blown out. People were panicking. Some were calling for their relatives, while others were in a state of complete shock. It was dark, night and everything was burning," Larysa said.
A neighbour of Larysa – a young man – was killed in the strike.
Olena, another resident of the building, said she hid with her family in the bathroom during the overnight attack. Their flat sustained significant damage, with the blast wave blowing out the doors.
"Everything in the flat went flying. The armoured door is lying right in the hallway. I hid in the bathroom with my child and my father. It was terrifying. We have no flat left, everything was blown apart. I just managed to hide my child in the bathroom," she said.
Another resident, Anastasiia, said she decided to go to a shelter early, so she was in a safe place during the attack. She said explosions could be heard in the shelter. Anastasiia then recognised her building from photos on social media and saw that it had been hit by a Russian missile.
"When the air-raid warning is issued, you don't have time to get to a shelter, and if you end up outside afterwards, it would mean certain death. We're not allowed back into our flats because it's too dangerous. But from the windows you can guess the scale of the destruction," she said.
Olha, another citizen affected by the Russian attack, was searching for a dog at the site of the attack – a border collie left with her by her son while he serves in the military.
"One bang. Two bangs. I was sitting in the kitchen. My son is at the front, his border collie is with me, and a cat too. I don't remember how I grabbed just my phone and ran into the corridor – the blast wave blew out the doors. I have two doors. We barely got out. She ran ahead of me and disappeared. I've been walking around looking for her the whole time," Olha told Radio Liberty.
Kyiv police officers told how they rescued a 51-year-old man. He was trapped under rubble after a ballistic missile strike on a warehouse. The man worked as a security guard.
Officers carefully extracted the man and carried him on a stretcher to a safe location. He was in a semi-conscious state and had numerous shrapnel and laceration wounds. He received medical treatment.
Background: On the morning of 14 August, nine-year-old Hlib Kovtunenko and his mother, 29-year-old Olha, were killed when Russia struck their home with two jet-powered drones.

articles.title: Zelensky slaps new sanctions on Moscow's war machine, Russian propagandists, and former Ukrainian officials
articles.body:
Russian children's cartoon targeted in Zelensky's latest sanctions against Moscow's war machine
Ukraine imposed new sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex, propaganda machine, and other targets on Aug. 20, according to a series of decrees signed by President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The updated sanctions list includes former Ukrainian lawmaker and Party of Regions member Yurii Ivanyushchenko and the creators of the animated Russian children's series "Masha and the Bear."
Zelensky signed four sanctions decrees on Aug. 20, the Presidential Office reported. One goes after companies and individuals linked to Russia's defense industry. It imposes restrictions on 28 Russian citizens, 36 Russian company, and one Chinese firm.
"We continue to systematically identify and restrict the activities of companies working for the Russian military-industrial complex," Presidential Sanctions Commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said.
"We expect our partners to support these efforts ... Sanctions should not only highlight involvement in the Russian war machine but also effectively deprive it of resources and international connections."
Some of the targeted individuals and entities listed in this decree are involved in sanctions evasion schemes and the supply of high-precision industrial equipment, tools, and parts. Others are connected to drone research, the production and repair of specialized military equipment, and software development for Russian security forces.
read also
Another decree takes aim at five companies owned by the sanctioned Russian aluminum giant Rusal. Nine Russian citizens affiliated with the designated companies are also listed.
The companies and individuals are linked to imports of alumina and other raw materials that help Russia produce missiles, artillery, military aircraft, and other weapons, the Presidential Office said.
A third sanctions decree targets 45 individuals and eight entities alleged to promote Russia's full-scale invasion and occupation of Ukrainian territory. These include Ivanyuschenko, a former member of Ukraine's parliament.
Ivanyushchenko belonged to the pro-Russian Party of Regions, which was previously led by ousted President Viktor Yanukovych and is now banned in Ukraine. A close ally of Yanukovych, Ivanyuschenko was allegedly behind the kidnapping, beating, and abduction of activists during the EuroMaidan Revolution.
Companies tied to Ivanyushchenko are currently operating in Russian-occupied Crimea, the Presidential Office said. He has allegedly visited Russia multiple times since the full-scale war began and maintains connections to "Russia's criminal and business circles."
Ivanyushchenko is also under criminal investigation involving a scheme to seize and legalize state-owned land.
read also
Zelensky's fourth decree singles out an unusual target: the popular Russian children's cartoon "Masha and the Bear," which has an international audience.
The decree imposes sanctions on five Russian citizens and four organizations involved in the creation and distribution of the series, including the screenwriter, director, and producer. The measures also target the animation studio Animaccord, as well as its founder and CEO.
Under these sanctions, Animaccord is prohibited from disseminating media in Ukraine. The measures also stipulate that the Ukrainian government may block "Masha and the Bear" — including its Ukrainian, Russian, and English versions — on YouTube and other sites.
The program "spreads pro-Russian narratives disguised as children's content," the Presidential Office said. 
"We must respond specifically to Russian propaganda, especially when it targets children and is disseminated through major international platforms," Sanctions Commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said. 
Individuals and entities designated under the new sanctions will be subject to asset freezes, trade restrictions, travel bans, and other penalties. Kyiv will work to synchronize the latest sanctions package with its international partners, the Presidential Office said.

articles.title: Drone Crashes Near Romania’s Border With Ukraine
articles.body:
On the night of August 20, a drone crashed in Romania near the border with Ukraine during a massive Russian attack on the Odesa region, the country’s defense ministry reported.
At 2:23 a.m., the radar surveillance system detected a group of aerial targets near the border with Ukraine.
Two Spanish Air and Space Force EF-18 fighter jets were scrambled to monitor the situation. Romanian military forces also deployed an IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter.
The drone entered Romanian airspace approximately 13 kilometers east of the city of Galați.
At 3:24 a.m., the crew of a Romanian helicopter reported that an aerial target had crashed approximately 4 kilometers northeast of the village of Grindu in Tulcea County.
The drone crashed in a remote area. After the crash, a fire broke out, which eventually went out on its own.
There have been no reports of casualties or property damage. Military personnel were dispatched to the crash site to secure the area. The air raid alert was lifted at 3:52 a.m.
On the morning of August 16, a Spanish EF-18 conducting a NATO air patrol mission shot down a drone that had entered Romanian airspace from Moldova.
This was already the fourth UAV shot down over Romania in 2026. On July 24, 25, and 26, Romanian F-16s shot down three Russian drones that had violated the country’s airspace.
In addition, on August 14, a Russian Shahed-type strike drone crashed in a wooded area near the Romanian village of Greci in Tulcea County, approximately 18 km from the Ukrainian border. It caused no casualties or material damage and was later destroyed in a controlled detonation.
The Romanian Ministry of National Defence stated that radar surveillance systems did not detect the air target because it was flying at a very low altitude.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed four decrees enacting decisions by the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine on imposing sanctions against enterprises in Russia’s military-industrial complex, companies belonging to the sanctioned "Rusal" group, collaborators, senior Russian officials, and the authors and distributors of the animated series "Masha and the Bear," UNN reports, citing the Office of the President.

articles.title: Russian Shaheds hit near Moldova-border crossing, burn food cargo, and black out 13,000 in Odesa Oblast
articles.body:
Russian strikes in southern Odesa Oblast overnight into 20 August left 13,000 utility customers without power, Odesa Oblast head Oleh Kiper reported. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said drones attacked a checkpoint on Ukraine’s border with Moldova.
Russia has intensified attacks on southern Ukraine’s Danube region, where ports and transport routes lie close to Moldova and Romania. The spillover from the attacks has forced these neighboring countries to close airspace, scramble aircraft, and shoot drones down.
The Odesa Oblast Military Administration said Russian strikes disrupted power in several communities, and repair crews began restoration work. It did not identify damaged electrical equipment or say whether the grid had been shut down as a precaution. Two truck trailers carrying food caught fire at another location, but firefighters extinguished both blazes, the State Emergency Service said. No casualties were reported.
Zelenskyy did not identify which crossing was attacked or describe the damage. The Izmail District State Administration later reported that Russia attacked the Reni community with Shahed-136 drones. It recorded a hit on an unspecified site near the Reni–Giurgiulești international checkpoint.
People and freight cross between Ukraine and Moldova through checkpoints such as Reni–Giurgiulești. The district administration did not describe the damage or say whether the checkpoint remained open.
Russian attacks keep reaching Moldova
At 03:16 on 20 August, surveillance systems operated by Moldova’s National Army detected an unauthorized flight, public broadcaster Moldova1 reported.
The object was preliminarily identified as a Shahed-136/Geran-2, a long-range explosive drone used by Russia. It crossed from Ukraine near Kotlovyna in southwestern Odesa Oblast and flew toward Etulia in Moldova’s autonomous Gagauzia region. It returned to Ukrainian airspace at 03:22.
Similar incidents occurred earlier in August. An unidentified aerial object exploded in a Moldovan field 12 kilometers from Ukraine on 9 August. On 17 August, Moldova closed part of its airspace for 15 minutes after Ukraine’s Air Force warned that a Russian Banderol, a jet-powered missile-drone, had crossed from Odesa Oblast. The object later exploded near Talmaza.
Romania activates defenses
On 20 August, Romania’s Defense Ministry said its radars detected targets near Ukraine at 02:23 and scrambled two Spanish F-18s and a Romanian helicopter. A drone entered Romanian airspace east of Galați at 03:21 and crashed near Grindu at 03:24. Its impact started a fire that went out on its own. Romania reported no casualties or material damage.
Four days earlier, a Spanish F-18 shot down a drone that entered Romania from Moldova. NATO said it appeared to be Russian.
Russia has recently intensified attacks on Ukraine’s Danube ports and struck the Mayaky bridge connecting southern Ukraine with Moldova and Romania. Such attacks can disrupt Ukraine’s transport links and force neighboring militaries to react within minutes.

articles.title: What is Egypt's role in the new regional security order?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What is Egypt's role in the new regional security order?
Egypt's current absence from the collective security pact signed between Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia, dubbed the ‘Mecca Agreement’, has brought renewed attention to Egypt’s security strategy towards its regional allies and the wider region.
While speculation surrounding Egypt’s absence from the agreement abounds, understanding Cairo’s position requires looking beyond the Mecca Agreement.
Egypt’s regional security posture has historically been shaped by a preference for strategic flexibility, driven by the recognition that its interests often require maintaining relationships with competing regional and international actors.
Today, this approach is being tested by an increasingly volatile regional environment marked by state and non-state threats, from Israel’s expanding regional wars to the US-Israel-Iran war and its fallout.
The complexities of this geostrategic environment have compelled Cairo to emphasise diplomacy, mediation, and issue-based security cooperation over concrete, bloc-based alignments.
Its rapprochement with Turkey, expanding security ties with major regional players including Saudi Arabia, and maintenance of diplomatic backchannels with rival actors underscore Egypt’s efforts to diversify its security partnerships while preserving the flexibility to engage across regional fault lines.
Security through diplomacy
A 1955 telegram from the US Embassy in Cairo to the US Department of State documented a tense exchange between then Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser and then US Assistant Secretary of State George Allen over Egypt’s acquisition of Czechoslovak arms.
During the exchange, Nasser expressed doubts about Washington’s reliability as a security partner and raised concerns about Israel’s growing influence and territorial ambitions, particularly the influence of the Herut party, the predecessor to today’s Likud.
The exchange reflects a key feature of Egyptian strategic thinking. Cairo has long been sceptical of overreliance on a single external security umbrella, preferring instead to preserve room for manoeuvre.
That instinct remains salient in Cairo’s approach today. "Egypt has largely focused on managing and balancing its bilateral relationships with all major regional players to address growing instability and threats,” Liam Karr, Africa Team Lead at the Critical Threats Project, told The New Arab.
Egypt’s security is increasingly being tested by instability beyond its immediate borders, primarily driven by Israel’s expanding regional wars and now compounded by the US-Israel-Iran war. Previously assumed to be relatively shielded from these developments, Egypt has increasingly found itself directly exposed to their consequences.
Israel’s war on Gaza heightened Egyptian threat perceptions, particularly amid Israeli calls at the time for the displacement of Palestinians into Sinai, a scenario Cairo repeatedly identified as a red line.
The war also brought Israeli incursions closer to Egyptian territory. Throughout the war, Israel repeatedly asserted control over the Philadelphi Corridor, a narrow strip along the Egypt-Gaza border whose security arrangements have been shaped by the 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty and subsequent agreements.
“Egypt’s threat perception has been shaped particularly by Israel’s unilateral security expansionism. This perception led to a greater emphasis on mediation across regional fault lines, while balancing against Cairo’s rivals, first and foremost Israel,” Ahmed Aboudouh, Associate Fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, told The New Arab.
Egypt’s response focused heavily on diplomacy. Alongside Qatar, Cairo maintained a central role in efforts to mediate between Israel and Hamas, positioning itself as an intermediary capable of communicating with multiple sides.
Earlier this month, US special envoy Jared Kushner met a Hamas delegation led by Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt, in a rare direct high-level meeting, to discuss implementation of the Board of Peace’s roadmap, namely the question of Hamas’s disarmament.
A durable end to the war on Gaza is vital to Egypt’s economic and security stability, particularly as the conflict continues to generate pressure along its border and across the Red Sea. Egypt’s economic vulnerabilities have raised the stakes. The Suez Canal, one of the country’s main sources of foreign currency, saw revenues collapse by roughly two-thirds at the height of Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping.
The resumption of attacks on Red Sea shipping and rising regional tensions stemming from the US-Israel-Iran war further jeopardise Egypt’s economic security. Cairo also remains heavily reliant on Gulf investment and financial support, making stability across the Gulf and Red Sea increasingly inseparable from its own economic security.
The Egyptian economy has, however, shown some signs of recovery. In July, the IMF reinforced confidence in Egypt’s economic reform program, unlocking an additional $1.8 billion in funds after Cairo completed its latest review. That said, underlying vulnerabilities remain.
The widening geography of the US-Israel-Iran war was underscored in late July, when a drone struck Egypt’s Damietta port. The incident marked the first attack on Egyptian territory since the outbreak of the war, illustrating the interconnectedness of regional conflicts and directly exposing Egypt to new security threats. It also highlighted the urgency of reaching a durable resolution.
Egypt’s diplomatic leverage derives in large part from its ability to maintain relationships across divides. Earlier this year, Egypt used its diplomatic backchannel with the IRGC, an increasingly prominent decision-making actor in Iran, to help preserve a line of contact during a moment of heightened tension. Given the trajectory of regional dynamics, these channels are likely to remain important.
Egypt has also demonstrated a willingness to extend military support to its regional partners. During Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi’s visit to Abu Dhabi in May, he visited an Egyptian fighter detachment stationed in the UAE comprising Rafale jets and Egyptian pilots, alongside reports of Egyptian defensive deployments in Saudi Arabia.
Gulf security is closely aligned with Egyptian interests, but Cairo’s current absence from the Mecca agreement may reflect a recognition of the risks that a more hardened posture could invite, as well as a preference for maintaining strategic balance.
Issue-based cooperation over bloc alignment
Egypt maintains robust security relationships with all three members of the Mecca Agreement. Its current absence from the pact should therefore not be interpreted as a rejection of closer regional security cooperation.
Egypt and Turkey have considerably expanded their security cooperation as part of their broader political rapprochement. In June, the two countries conducted joint F-16 drills, the first exercise of its kind in almost two decades, building on the momentum generated by their 2025 joint maritime exercise, “Sea of Friendship.”
Ankara and Cairo have also pledged greater coordination on regional files including Sudan, Libya, and Gaza. Additionally, defence-industrial cooperation has expanded. Ankara and Cairo signed agreements worth approximately $350 million earlier this year aimed primarily at expanding joint production efforts.
These initiatives serve Egypt’s immediate defence needs while simultaneously enhancing regional strategic autonomy.
Cairo’s relationship with Riyadh is similarly deep. Egypt was among the 14 founding members of the Saudi-led Red Sea security maritime force. Its participation also builds on extensive experience in collective maritime security initiatives, including its current command, for the second time, of the Combined Maritime Forces’ Combined Task Force-153, the Red Sea focused task force.
“Egypt wants to be a central leader to regional approaches in its backyard, as shown by its involvement in the Sudan Quad, various multilateral security initiatives in the Red Sea, and the Libya and Palestine peace processes,” Karr told The New Arab.
Diversified partnerships
Participation in a formal collective security pact could strengthen deterrence, but it could also narrow Egypt’s room for manoeuvre and constrain its ability to mediate across regional divides.
“Egypt will maintain its cautious, defensive and risk-averse approach to avoid antagonising any party with leverage to pressure its direct national interests,” said Aboudouh.
Egypt will likely continue diversifying its security partnerships rather than committing to formal blocs. In line with this posture, China and Egypt are currently hosting the second iteration of their joint aerial exercise, "Eagles of Civilisation," from mid-August to early September, following the inaugural exercise held in 2025.
Strategically, Cairo will also have to guard against military overstretch as it manages simultaneous pressure across two turbulent fronts, the Middle East and the Nile Basin. Ethiopia's plans for three additional dams on the Nile have already drawn strong opposition from Cairo.
Managing these competing pressures will reinforce Egypt’s preference for diversified partnerships and strategic flexibility, allowing it to deepen cooperation where its interests converge while avoiding overreliance on any single security partner.
Hana Elshehaby is a Senior Research Assistant for the Middle East Council on Global Affairs. She is also a Non-Resident Fellow at the Institute for Middle East Options

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine needs Patriot missiles, not gifts – we ready to buy weapons
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine needs additional missiles for its Patriot air defense systems, which partners can provide, and that Ukraine is ready to purchase them.
"We need missiles for the Patriot system; this is something only our partners can provide. At all levels, we are making it clear to them both our need and the fact that we know our partners can meet this need. We're not talking about gifts; this is about Ukraine's readiness to purchase weapons," Zelenskyy said in an evening address on Thursday.
According to the president, this requires appropriate political decisions from our partners, primarily the United States.
Zelenskyy also said that 16 people were killed as a result of the Russian strike, nearly 50 more were wounded, and over 200 facilities were damaged, including 86 residential buildings, a children's hospital, and social infrastructure facilities.
"We will definitely respond to this Russian strike, just as we have responded to other Russian strikes. We will respond in a fully just and far-reaching manner," the president said.

articles.title: North Korea has around 120 nuclear weapons: Seoul claims
articles.body:
ALBAWABA - South Korea's defence minister alleged on Thursday that its neighboring country, North Korea, is estimated to have around 80 to 120 nuclear weapons.
The announcement by Ahn Gyu-back came shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump said North Korea has 57 nuclear weapons.
"We usually estimate it to be around 80 to 120," Ahn Gyu-back said, telling lawmakers, as reported by AFP.
Days ago, Trump revealed intentions to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un later this year. The U.S. president suggested he and Kim were holding secret negotiations on Tuesday after unveiling that Washington would downgrade its participation in military exercises held by South Korea.
However, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s supreme leader, responded to Trump's desire to meet her brother, Kim, saying, "The United States' hostile policy toward the DPRK has not changed, and the United States and its followers are vigorously carrying out hostile military activities against the DPRK even at this very moment."

articles.title: Simultaneous Russian attack on NATO and Chinese operation in Taiwan would be very dangerous scenario - Dolhov
articles.body:
Simultaneous Russian attack on NATO and Chinese operation in Taiwan would be very dangerous scenario - Dolhov
At the same time, one of the most dangerous potential scenarios is the simultaneous outbreak of two large-scale crises—a Russian attack against a NATO member state and a Chinese operation against Taiwan. Ukrainian diplomat Ihor Dolhov expressed this view in his program “Ihor Dolhov’s Program,” which was released on Ukrinform’s YouTube channel.
He noted that Ukraine possesses Patriot anti-aircraft missile launchers but currently faces a shortage of missiles to counter Russian ballistic attacks. According to Dolhov, the problem with stocks of such missiles is not limited to Ukraine. “There are fewer of them in the United States. There are fewer of them in Europe. There are fewer of them in other countries,” the diplomat noted.
Dolhov attributes this situation, in particular, to the extensive use of American weapons during the Gulf War.
At the same time, Russia continues its massive attacks on Ukraine and is striking Ukrainian ports, creating additional risks not only to the country’s security but also to its economy. According to Dolhov, Russian strikes have significantly hampered exports through Black Sea ports, and a further blockade of Ukrainian agricultural exports could have consequences for global food security. “A humanitarian crisis, a food crisis due to a shortage of wheat and grains on the market. Russia is also threatening to freeze Ukraine out this winter,” the diplomat noted.
He emphasized that, at the same time, the international security situation is deteriorating: Russia is escalating its threats against European countries and Japan, while the war in the Middle East is diverting a significant portion of U.S. military resources.
According to Dolhov, this creates additional opportunities for China to increase pressure around Taiwan.
The diplomat cited the simultaneous outbreak of two large-scale crises—a Russian attack against one of the NATO member states and a Chinese operation against Taiwan—as one of the most dangerous potential scenarios. “And NATO will have no means to respond. Nor will the United States be able to help either Europe or Taiwan. They will be completely tied up in the war in the Persian Gulf,” Dolhov stated.
According to him, under such conditions, Europe must focus not only on finding a new format for negotiations but, above all, on strengthening its ability to deter Russia and compel it to engage in genuine negotiations.
Earlier, The Atlantic reported that NATO leadership is taking increasingly seriously the scenario of a simultaneous attack by Russia on Europe and by China on Taiwan. At the same time, the U.S. and NATO are not prepared for a simultaneous war with Russia and China.

articles.title: Ukraine’s air defense increasingly struggling to cope with Russian strikes — newspaper
articles.body:
NEW YORK, August 20. /TASS/. Ukraine’s air defense is becoming increasingly unable to repel Russian attacks, The New York Times reported.
According to the newspaper, recent strikes indicate the Russian military’s growing confidence in its ability to overcome the Ukrainian air defense systems.
Ukrainian military officials and politicians regularly speak of a shortage of air defense missiles and ask Western countries to increase deliveries of such weapons.
However, Russian security agencies previously told TASS that the Ukrainian military is facing serious shortages of missiles for their Patriot systems and may have a hidden stockpile of ammunition.

articles.title: Ukraine's Defence Intelligence provides Ukrainska Pravda with data on Russia's missile stockpiles and production rates
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defence Intelligence provides Ukrainska Pravda with data on Russia's missile stockpiles and production rates
Ukrainska Pravda has learned that Russia has no shortage of missiles and has the capacity to produce more than 200 cruise and ballistic missiles per month. Its largest stockpiles are made up of Oniks and Kalibr missiles as well as RM-48U missiles for S-400 air defence systems, which Russia has adapted for use against ground targets.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda article "Russia's missile stockpiles, and why it needs a new North Korean missile unit: what experts and Defence Intelligence of Ukraine say"
Details: Data provided to Ukrainska Pravda by Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) shows that Russia continues to maintain a high rate of missile production, in some cases exceeding its planned output.
Quote from the article: "Russia can, in total, produce more than 200 cruise and ballistic missiles a month. The main priority right now is the production of Iskander-M, Kh-101 and Kalibr missiles."
More details: DIU reported that Russia has around 600 Oniks missiles, 450 Kalibrs and 400 RM-48U ballistic missiles for S-400 systems.
As of 5 August, Russia had around 130 9M723 ballistic missiles for Iskander-M systems. Its stockpiles are estimated at around 120 Zircon missiles, 100 Kh-101 missiles and 50 Kinzhal missiles.
According to DIU data, as of July 2026, Russia also had around 50 North Korean KN-23, KN-24 and KN-30 ballistic missiles.
The article notes that Russia's military-industrial complex has a monthly production target of 60 9M723 missiles for Iskander-M systems. However, this target was exceeded in July, when 65 missiles were produced.
That same month, Russia produced 87 Kh-101 cruise missiles.
In addition, Russia manufactures around 50 RM-48U missiles for S-400 systems each month. Over the course of 2026, Russia plans to produce more than 480 RM-48U missiles – more than twice the number planned for 2025.
Background:
- Starting from 18:00 on 19 August, Russian forces attacked Kyiv Oblast with Oniks, Zircon and Iskander-M missiles and missiles fired from S-400 systems that approach their targets on a ballistic trajectory.
- Twelve people were killed and 34 others injured in the Russian attack on Kyiv.
