articles.title: MQ-9 Lost in Middle East Last Year Due to Chafed Wire: New Report
articles.body:
A frayed wire likely triggered stray voltage to shut off a fuel valve, causing the catastrophic loss of an MQ-9 Reaper drone last August, according to a new Air Force investigation report.
The aircraft, valued at $23.6 million, was destroyed in place. It is among at least 40 MQ-9s lost or shot down over the past 18 months.
Air Combat Command released the Accident Investigation Board report on Aug. 13, nearly a year after the Aug. 31, 2025, mishap. The exact location of the mishap was not disclosed—the report said only that it took place in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility.
The MQ-9 belonged to the 432nd Wing at Creech Air Force Base, Nev., while the pilot and sensor operator were from the 89th Attack Squadron at Ellsworth Air Force Base, S.D. The drone was returning from a mission to its base in the region and had been in the air nearly 19 hours when the engine shut off.
The drone automatically attempted to restart the twice, and the crew tried two manual restarts as well before the Reaper crashed to the ground. Operators tried for a soft landing to preserve the aircraft but were not successful.
After sorting through several options to avoid population centers and minimize damage, the crew selected a “relatively flat and isolated” piece of desert and tried to go in with the landing gear down, according to the report. But the crew lost contact with the aircraft as it descended below 2,000 feet.
The Reaper landed near the selected landing area, but “the force of the impact caused its landing gear to collapse,” according to the report. “Following the landing, sensitive equipment was removed from the [aircraft] and the remaining wreckage was demolished on site.”
The problem occurred on the aircraft’s first flight after its engine was replaced as part of a routine 3,000-hour engine inspection. During that inspection, personnel from contractor Honeywell noted three issues beyond normal wear:
- The propeller governor cable was chafed and replaced
- The fuel control unit was replaced with a new unit overhauled in April 2025, due to a missing log card
- The compressor seal was leaking and replaced
Notably, the inspection and replacement routine did not include removing the top cover from the fuel control unit, which regulates the flow of fuel to the engine—despite “known examples of the FCU sensor wire chafing,” according to MQ-9 manufacturer General Atomics. Honeywell personnel reported they had observed “a relay wire shorting and sparking” while servicing a different aircraft.
Based on data logs, investigators determined the MQ-9 engine experienced a spike in fuel flow just before plummeting to zero. General Atomics was able to recreate that sequence in its lab by suddenly closing the electrical fuel shutoff valve.
Those tests, combined with the known issue of the wires chafing inside the fuel control unit, led investigators to conclude the most likely explanation for the mishap was that a frayed wire inside the fuel control unit leaked enough voltage to trigger the fuel shutoff valve to close.
The board noted that while most U.S. Air Force aircraft are required to undergo some sort of check flight after their engine is replaced “to ensure the aircraft is airworthy and to test the flight integrity of all systems, particularly critical systems like those affecting engines,” the MQ-9 maintenance manual has no such requirement, the board said.
What’s more, investigators noted with surprise that a complete engine change is considered “routine maintenance” on MQ-9s, and that the crew controlling the drone was never informed that their aircraft had just received an entirely new engine.
The Accident Investigation Board cited inadequate planning and briefing and inadequate written standards as “relevant factors” in the mishap.
MQ-9 Losses
The MQ-9 mishap occurred during a relative lull in operations in the Middle East. Just months earlier, from March to May 2025, Operation Rough Rider sought to halt attacks on commercial shipping by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. The Houthis downed about a half dozen MQ-9s during that stretch using electro-optical/infrared surface-to-air missile systems, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported.
At least two dozen MQ-9s were subsequently lost during Operation Epic Fury against Iran starting in late February, some to air defense missiles and some struck on the ground.
By May, after a brief ceasefire took hold, the Air Force was down around 30 Reapers, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported. Hostilities began again in earnest by July, and the Washington Post reported last week that “at least 45” MQ-9s have been destroyed.
The Air Force reported having 230 MQ-9s in its inventory at the start of fiscal 2025; one year later, it had just 182. In May, Lt. Gen. David Tabor, Air Force deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, said the fleet was down to around 135 aircraft.
Air Force officials have praised the performance of the MQ-9 in the Iran conflict, saying it has accounted for many of the thousands of strikes conducted during the campaign and gathered valuable intelligence. Some have also hinted that commanders have sometimes employed them in ways that put the drones at greater risk.
With the fleet shrinking, leaders are discussing how to replace the losses. Options include acquiring the few remaining MQ-9As from General Atomics, buying the larger MQ-9Bs now being built, or developing replacement platforms. Among the alternatives backed by some on the Air Staff is a project jointly pursued by the Defense Innovation Unit and the Air Force. The so-called “massed modular aircraft,” or MMA is conceived as an “attritable” aircraft whose loss is treated more like a munition than a aircraft. Vendors have offered proposals and an acquisition official said in July that one or competitors could be selected by the end of 2026.

articles.title: Russia still has 50 Kinzhal missiles after pausing production, HUR claims
articles.body:
Russia still has about 50 Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles in its arsenal, despite pausing production of the munition in order to improve its accuracy, Ukraine's Military Intelligence (HUR) has claimed.
The Kinzhal is a modified version of the Iskander ballistic missile, which is launched by specially modified MiG-31K interceptor jets. Over the course of the full-scale war they have regularly been used to attack Ukraine.
"As of July 2026, the Russian Federation has about 50 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles and about 50 North Korean ballistic missiles of the KN-23 series, including the KN-24 and KN-30 variants," HUR said in a statement to Ukrainska Pravda.
Leaked Russian documents obtained by Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi revealed each Kinzhal costs around $4.5 million to produce. The documents also said Russia had planned to produce 144 units in 2025.
Production of the Kinzhal has been suspended since April 2026. The accuracy of the munition had been negatively affected by Ukrainian jamming and GPS spoofing, according to aviation industry expert Arkady Dotsenko.
"When we put up our EW (electronic warfare) wall, of 59 launched Kinzhals, only one landed. All the rest were suppressed," one commander of a Ukrainian electronic warfare unit told the Kyiv Independent in April.
Russia has redirected resources from Kinzhal production toward producing other missile types, HUR claims.
"Reorienting production resources to other missile systems allows Russia to maintain necessary production rates and ensure the regular use of missiles against Ukraine," it said in their statement.

articles.title: Romania destroys drone near offshore gas project, blames Russia
articles.body:
(AFP Photo)
A Romanian F-16 fighter jet on Aug. 20 destroyed a marine drone near an offshore gas project, with Romania's president blaming Russia for the latest incident involving the NATO member bordering Ukraine.
Unauthorized drone activity has become increasingly frequent in recent months across eastern European countries as Ukraine fights off a Russian invasion launched in 2022, with both countries increasingly relying on drone warfare.
In the latest incident, the drone that was destroyed was "loaded with explosives" and did not originate from Ukraine, Defense Minister Radu Miruta said on Facebook.
"I strongly condemn the escalation of such irresponsible incidents on the part of the Russian Federation," Romanian President Nicusor Dan said on X.
The drone was spotted at 6:28 am local time (0328 GMT) by a commercial vessel, hundreds of meters from the offshore gas project Neptun Deep and 80 nautical miles east of the Black Sea city of Constanta, according to a press release from the defense ministry.
Two Romanian F-16 aircraft were deployed to respond, and one of them destroyed it.
Hundreds of people are currently working at Neptun Deep, according to the government. Neptun Deep is due to start production in 2027.
NATO has shot down four aerial drones in Romania recently, with the latest incident happening during last weekend.
The eastern European country also reported an aerial drone crash on Aug. 20 following Russian strikes on Ukraine.
It fell in an unpopulated area four kilometers (2.5 miles) northeast of the village of Grindu in eastern Romania, close to the border.
No casualties were reported.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Aug. 20 urged a global response to Moscow's "escalation" of the four-year war after Russian bombardments killed at least 16 people in Kiev and surrounding areas overnight.

articles.title: 'We will tear you to pieces': Indian general warns Erdogan about pact with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan
articles.body:
Retired Indian Maj.-Gen. Gagan Deep Bakshi warned that the growing alignment among Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan could pose a strategic threat to India, while stressing that New Delhi would not sacrifice its ties with Iran to accommodate Israel’s security concerns.
Speaking to the New Delhi-based network, Republic World, Bakshi argued that the emergence of what he calls a "Sunni NATO" in the Middle East is a source of strategic concern for India.
At the same time, he sent a clear message to Israel: The alliance between the two countries is important, but New Delhi will not give up its interests with Iran simply because of the war between Jerusalem and Tehran.
According to Bakshi, the agreement that took shape in Mecca among Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan has created a new regional reality from India's perspective. "A Sunni NATO comprising Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan has been established in the Middle East, in Mecca, and that is a serious cause for concern," he said.
Bakshi stressed that, from India's perspective, Shi'ite Iran serves as an important counterweight to Pakistan.
Iran as a counterweight to Pakistan
"We very much need Shi'ite Iran to be on our side because Pakistan is our primary security headache. China may be the main threat, but together with it, Pakistan is our biggest security headache," he said.
Bakshi compared the threat Iran represents in Israel's eyes with that posed by Pakistan from India's perspective.
"Iran does not have even a single nuclear bomb, and yet it is perceived as an existential threat to Israel. And what about Pakistan? A fundamentalist, jihadist Islamic state that possesses 180 nuclear warheads," he claimed.
He added that India had not seen Israel display similar concern over Pakistan's nuclear arsenal.
"We have not seen Israel losing sleep over the bombs in Pakistan's hands because they are considered a threat only to India," he said.
According to Bakshi, the rapprochement between Ankara and Islamabad is not merely theoretical. He cited Turkish assistance to Pakistan during Operation Sindoor, claiming that Turkey supplied it with nearly 1,000 unmanned aerial vehicles and helped operate them.
"This was already a 'Sunni NATO,' with or without an agreement. Turkey and Pakistan are already in an undeclared practical alliance," he said.
Bakshi also noted that during the confrontation, Turkey sent a warship to the port of Karachi, arguing that this was another expression of the close security ties between the two countries.
"Turkey has the largest army in NATO," he said, while questioning its ability to intervene directly in a war between India and Pakistan because of the geographical distance.
According to Bakshi, any Turkish force attempting to come to Pakistan's aid would have to travel through the Mediterranean Sea and the Arabian Sea.
"The Indian Navy can tear apart any Turkish armada that tries to come to Pakistan's aid," he said.
India will not sacrifice its interests with Iran
A central part of Bakshi's remarks was directed squarely at Israel. He stressed that India views Israel as a friend, but would not agree to subordinate its own interests to Israeli needs, particularly when it comes to Iran.
"I am afraid that at some point Israel will also have to be sensitive to Indian concerns," he said. "We are not the 51st state of the United States, and for that matter we are also not an appendage or client state of Israel. We are friends, certainly. But vassals? No, sir."
"You cannot simply whistle and make our senior leaders go here and there, and ask us to sacrifice our interests," he said.
Bakshi specifically addressed possible pressure on India to distance itself from Iran because of the war.
"You cannot tell us: Throw Iran away because you are at war with it. When it comes to Iran, you cannot ask us to sacrifice our interests."
According to Bakshi, relations with Iran are vital to India economically and geostrategically as well. He pointed to the possibility of purchasing Iranian oil at low prices, refining it at Indian refineries, and subsequently exporting the products to other markets.
Beyond that, he stressed Iran's importance as an overland route for India.
"Iran provides India with the land bridge to Central Asia and the land bridge to Afghanistan, and these are of vital importance to us."
India cannot afford to give up those routes because of the war between Israel and Iran, he said.
"We cannot close these land routes because Israel is at war with Iran."
Bakshi concluded that the friendship between India and Israel remains important, but that from New Delhi's perspective, it has clear limits when major security and economic interests are at stake. Against the backdrop of growing ties between Turkey and Pakistan, and Indian concerns over a broader Sunni alliance, he believes that India's relationship with Iran is becoming more important, not less.

articles.title: Russia’s Supreme Court threw Yabloko off September’s Duma ballot. The antiwar party has just 4,000 members, but 8,000 people have applied to join in the last two weeks.
articles.body:
Russia’s Supreme Court threw Yabloko off September’s Duma ballot. The antiwar party has just 4,000 members, but 8,000 people have applied to join in the last two weeks.
Yabloko’s election campaign became Russia’s biggest political story of the summer before it had even properly begun: the Supreme Court removed the party from the ballot, and hundreds of young people came out to support Yabloko. Meanwhile, one of Yabloko’s leaders, Lev Shlosberg, was sentenced to 11 years on trumped-up charges. Amid all that, the party is riding an unprecedented surge of popularity: thousands of people have already submitted applications to join, and Yabloko has picked up hundreds of thousands of new followers on social media. Bereg, a cooperative of independent journalists, spoke with Kirill Goncharov, head of Yabloko’s Moscow branch, about how the party reads its own popularity and what it intends to do with it. Meduza is translating the piece in full.
The interview started a little later than planned, and Kirill Goncharov opened by explaining the delay.
— I asked to push things back five minutes because a hearing was going on at the same time for a young man, Artem Kuznetsov. We don’t know him personally, just as we don’t know most of the detainees who were outside the Supreme Court, but one way or another, we’re responsible for him even though we’ve never met. He was given 14 days in jail.
After the hearing, my mind switched completely from the campaign to human rights work, so I haven’t even had time to process what happened. Something tectonic has probably happened, some kind of tectonic shift, but it’s too soon to draw conclusions, especially since the process is still unfolding.
The [State Duma election] campaign is still ahead of us — [Yabloko’s] candidates in single-mandate districts, party lists in the regions. In that sense, we’re continuing the campaign, and we’re feeling a real burst of optimism, no matter what.
— What exactly does Yabloko’s assistance to the detainees involve?
— We find lawyers and pay for them, which isn’t cheap given how many people have been detained. Sometimes we have to find them in the middle of the night — at two or three in the morning it turns out that someone is being held at a temporary detention center or a police station. The day before yesterday, we launched a Telegram bot to field requests.
We’re following the cases and getting the word out — people travel to see the detainees, form support groups, and pack care packages.
Two days ago, one of the detainees sent me a private message: “Thanks for getting the word out — the cops were talking about it, and it helped. They knew they couldn’t rough us up.” That made me think I should write about this more often, since it can actually help.
— How many people has Yabloko given legal assistance to?
— Everyone who’s had charges filed against them. That’s 10 to 12 people. At first things went reasonably well. From what we heard, police detained people en masse on the first day, August 17, and then let them all go without filing any charges. It felt like they’d simply decided to detain everyone outside the court to break up the line and demoralize people, then let them all go without charges.
But it turned out that charges were mostly filed against people who had come to the August 10 hearing [on removing Yabloko from the State Duma election]. Many of them weren’t even there on August 17 — the police detained them at home, near their homes, or elsewhere, tracking them down on surveillance cameras. They’re getting hit with either organizing an unauthorized rally or so-called obstruction of traffic.
— What are your impressions from talking with the young people who came to the courthouse to support Yabloko on August 10 and 17?
— I don’t know if you were around for the Moscow rallies of the 2000s and 2010s. You’d show up and run into Mikhail Shneider, Roman Dobrokhotov, Oleg Kozlovsky… say hello, chat for a bit — it was a kind of roving rally.
But now it’s a completely new crowd, and I mean that in a good way. Young, driven, really fired up. Some of them probably haven’t figured out yet what country they’re living in. Many are 18 or 19. But they already feel suffocated, because the one time they decided to go and vote, they were stripped of the chance before they even got there.
They can’t explain it to themselves, let alone to anyone else. They watch what’s happening in the courtroom and understand it’s a huge injustice. A lot of them lose heart. Many cried outside the court — and that’s not a figure of speech. They really cried.
After the August 10 hearing, my colleagues and I went to a fast-food place. We walk in, and the whole crowd is already there — about 50 people who’d been standing outside the court. Everyone was crying, coming up to us, asking what would happen next. I even said to my colleagues, “God, why did we come in here?”
I genuinely feel for these people. Fine, the authorities are trying to shut Yabloko out of the election — but on top of Yabloko, you’re shutting out tens of thousands of voters. Nationwide, we’re confident we would have won several million votes from people who chose to stay in Russia, to live and work here. And they don’t have many other outlets for civic life or self-expression.
Elections were the last outlet left. The authorities always told us: “Rallies are bad, pickets are bad. Run in elections, appeal to society through elections. And if society backs you, fine, we won’t resist.” So we ran in the election — and got the same result.
So when the authorities shut such a huge number of people out of public life, and then turn aggressive toward children outside the courthouse… These really are children. The people there were 17 to 19 years old. Even I felt very old in that crowd [Goncharov is 34].
I don’t recognize a single meme they use, and I don’t know what some of their words mean. And these are finally kids who, unlike the generations before them, want to take part in politics, and right away they get shut out.
I think this is a major civic and humanitarian catastrophe for our country. In the long run, the authorities won’t achieve anything good by shutting so many people out of the [political] process. Yes, they’ve won for now, but it’s a Pyrrhic victory. No one knows what it will turn into in a year, or two, or three — but it certainly won’t be anything good.
— Was there even a sliver of hope the court might rule differently?
— On the legal merits, yes. The defense’s position was absolutely ironclad. Every lawyer we corresponded with — even those outside the case who knew our arguments from the preparation stage — agreed it was well argued. What’s more, not even an ordinary Moscow district court would have accepted the Rodina party’s lawsuit if the case weren’t politicized and the decision weren’t coming from senior officials. The court, to put it mildly, didn’t stick to the tradition of adversarial proceedings.
— I want to ask not about the legal grounds — those are clear — but about the political reality. What did Grigory Yavlinsky say, as someone who knows all the key political figures and can see how events will unfold?
— I won’t relay our conversation, but of course no one had any illusions. Personally, I didn’t expect us to be registered at all.
I’ve been in politics since 2010. I remember the protests of 2011 and 2019 — I took part in all of them and organized some myself. A year ago I was already saying big protests were coming, because the protest trend was building. This past winter, I told colleagues that 2011 could repeat itself.
What I felt in 2011 and 2019 was very close to what’s happening now, except that now there are more social problems on top of it: the attacks on Wildberries, the drone attacks on oil refineries, the fuel crisis that followed, and the campaign against the internet.
All of that is pushing people into politics. Eventually even people far removed from politics start asking about root causes and how to end it all. And it turns out what’s needed is a ceasefire and peace. So who’s speaking up for peace in Russia right now? People google the question, find Yabloko, and subscribe to its channels. Yabloko’s leaders repeat that [call for peace] every day. And people start supporting the party.
Yesterday I was walking down the street and about five people walked past me and there was a bit of a commotion. They looked at me and started smiling. I figured they’d recognized me — it’s been happening a lot over the past two weeks. People recognize me and come up to me, especially in the metro.
— I wanted to ask what you attribute Yabloko’s rapid rise in popularity to, but it seems you’ve already answered that.
— There was a match between what people were hoping for and what we stand for. Our position has never changed, but what people expect is always shaped by context. The context of summer 2026 is a public demand for peace — and we’re the only ones who can meet that demand, because we called for a ceasefire from the very beginning.
In 2022, everyone piled on us for those exact same words. Yabloko took so much criticism — literally from the people who support us today. Now they say the whole opposition has consolidated around Yabloko. But they consolidated around us behind the very same slogans they criticized us for four years ago, when they called us “Kremlin agents.”
— Who criticized you?
— I won’t name names.
— Representatives of the non-systemic opposition?
— Yes.
— Doesn’t it sting to hear the opposition abroad argue that Yabloko isn’t oppositional enough?
— Be my guest. We’re not in anyone’s way. They’re welcome to come back and be more oppositional themselves. I just don’t know what the criteria for “oppositional” are. Two Yabloko deputy chairs are sitting in prison — one got seven years, the other 11. Isn’t that a criterion?
All right, let’s take another criterion. Not a single party leader was able to run in this election. It’s honestly unclear now why the authorities bothered, since in the end they let no one in at all. But for a full year they hounded the party chairman and all his deputies with fines, and now every one of them carries a fine that bars them from running. Isn’t that a criterion? Not oppositional enough?
All right. They removed us from the election. Isn’t that a criterion too?
Well, excuse us, but we’re not a guerrilla unit — we’re never going to take up arms. We believe in evolutionary change. But that’s not a measure of how oppositional you are. Honestly, I’m just tired. I’ve stopped arguing with people who say we’re not oppositional enough. Fine, I get it. Come here and be oppositional yourselves — we’re not stopping you.
— And yet when word came that Yabloko had been registered, Ilya Yashin, Vladimir Kara-Murza, Yulia Navalnaya, and other opposition figures living abroad backed you en masse. Did you expect that kind of unified response?
— We hadn’t really thought about it, and we didn’t expect it — not because we doubted they’d support us, but because that wasn’t part of our plan. We’re focused on the people who live in Russia.
— In recent weeks, TikTok has been flooded with videos of teenagers backing Yabloko, set to a song by the singer Yolka. Did the hype frighten you?
— No, these are great kids. The hype may have frightened Yolka, since as far as I know she isn’t especially oppositional — at least she wasn’t before. Maybe now, with hundreds of thousands of these videos out there, they’ve finally won her over. But it didn’t frighten us.
The other day I heard from a good friend in Montenegro who had to leave Russia after all this started: “Kirill, could you and I have imagined back in 2016 that Yabloko would become the trendiest political party in Russia in 2026?” At first I said, “Of course not, we couldn’t have.” Then I thought, “Damn, actually, maybe we could have.” We’ve been doing this for many years — we never left, never gave up, never abandoned the party, just kept doing what we do. Somewhere deep down, we were probably waiting for this moment. We were just too embarrassed to say it out loud to each other, because it seemed crazy and abnormal.
But that’s exactly what we worked for — for people to learn about our position, and for that position to reach a mass audience. We never doubted it could be popular, but it had never been a mass position before. That always surprised me, because there’s nothing to argue about here. It’s like arguing over whether a person needs two arms and two legs. Everything we propose in our platform is vital: human rights, freedom, and choice.
We’re not orthodox militarists, communists, or fascists. We’re normal people who demand to be treated normally. No more, no less. And people like that are the majority in Russia.
That is precisely why they pulled [Yabloko’s party list] from the election.
— I get the impression you’re a little euphoric about this influx of support. Is that true?
— No, not me, definitely not. Let me explain why. Yesterday we held a party commission meeting — that’s where we interview people who want to join. We have a huge number of applications.
People are handing over their passport details and aren’t afraid to do it. We tell every one of them: thank you, this is incredibly brave, we appreciate it enormously. But it matters to us that this isn’t a byproduct of the hype, because by fall that wave [of hype] could pass. What will you do then? Will you still want to be a party member once the hype fades, or not? That matters to us, and we’re not wearing rose-colored glasses — we understand what kind of moment this is. It’s like the World Cup, when everyone suddenly starts rooting for some national team. It’s the same now. In politics, elections are the World Cup. Everyone got swept up and picked a team to cheer for. What matters is that it doesn’t pass with time.
We don’t feel euphoria — we feel joy at what’s happening. We really are glad when people are willing to state their position, when they aren’t afraid and they support us. It would be foolish not to be.
— How many new membership applications have come in altogether, and how many members did Yabloko have before this?
— Over the past two weeks, we’ve received 8,000 applications. The party has about 4,000 members.
— Wow. So the party could potentially triple in size.
— Yes, and the whole campaign is still ahead of us.
— That could substantially change the mood among party members and the party’s direction.
— Yes, 100%. And that’s exactly what we’re urging people to do. We can sense that a lot of people are demoralized and disappointed right now over our removal. One thing that can keep people going is staying in a circle of like-minded people. It’ll do people as much good psychologically as politically.
— Aren’t you worried that another 200% will join, bringing their own vision of politics, and eventually pull the party in a radically different direction?
— We’ll bring them in. I oversee the federal party school, which works with young people and runs educational projects. On top of that, they don’t become party members right away — it takes two years, which gives us time to work with them.
— And to block them from joining if they don’t match your values?
— If people don’t fit, they sense it themselves and don’t put themselves or us through it. But that doesn’t happen very often.
— Well, there have been cases of people being expelled from Yabloko.
— There have been expulsions. That’s exactly why we introduced the two-year probationary period — so people can figure out how well we suit them, and we can figure out how well they suit us. But the young people coming in now are wonderful. We see them, we talk with all of them, and I have no doubt they’ll be a great addition.
— Have you measured your rise in popularity any other way? Through social media, maybe?
— Yes, of course. When it all started, the first place we looked was social media, because searches [for Yabloko] on Yandex were outpacing searches for every other party combined. Our channels started picking up subscribers. The biggest jump came on the party’s Telegram channel, which has almost 308,000 [new] subscribers; before the party was registered for the election in July, it had 12,000.
We were always accused of not knowing how to work online. This campaign showed that when the conditions exist, we can. When they don’t, nobody can. And there’s still YouTube, Instagram, and the personal social media accounts of Yabloko’s leaders.
— Has Yabloko conducted its own polling?
— No, we didn’t have the money for it.
— I’ve heard from sources close to Yabloko’s election campaign that this sudden popularity in Russia left the party in a mild stupor. Is that true?
— I don’t know. The party is big. Maybe someone went into a stupor, someone else into a coma, and someone else had a stroke. Everyone’s different. But people are happy. They didn’t expect this.
Last winter, I talked with a colleague from Yabloko, a very serious man. We argued — we had two different points of view. I said people could get political very soon. The authorities were already blocking the internet and Telegram. He told me Yabloko would never make it back into the State Duma and would never clear the [5%] threshold, because that had never happened in history.
I said history isn’t linear. Just because something hasn’t happened doesn’t mean it never will. He came back at me with examples, tables, expert opinion, and analysis, all to prove it never would.
And here we are. There were different opinions then — and now everyone has different emotions.
— This new support is major political capital, but it’s very dangerous in the current climate. What’s happening inside the party? There must be debate over how to proceed — surely there are veterans in Yabloko who want to fight to preserve the party at any cost.
— No, there’s no such debate. Preserving the party doesn’t mean turning support away. Any party should be fighting for people’s support.
I can point to my speech at the party congress — held before Yabloko was registered — in which I described exactly what ended up happening: that a window of opportunity would open, that the political reality would shift. Even then I was saying that a lot of people were coming to us; you could already feel that trend. So nothing surprising happened, as far as I’m concerned. And my colleagues don’t see it as some kind of challenge either. For everyone, this is simply a new stage in our development.
— Still, there’s a sense of a turning point in the party’s history. You yourself mentioned tectonic shifts. Yabloko has always been a fairly systemic opposition force — and that’s what kept it alive until today. But now it seems the party can no longer exist by its old rules. You don’t agree?
— No, I don’t. This is an argument about what “systemic” even means. Every party that exists in Russia came out in support of the ”special military operation” [the Kremlin’s term for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine]. We didn’t — from the very start. By the standards of what counts as systemic, where do we fit? Are we somehow still systemic? Hardly. Our leadership is sitting in prison.
By the system’s own standards, we were always non-systemic. We never fit into their worldview or their political spectrum. There was just this trend where you always had to knock Yabloko for being systemic. One popular figure said it, everyone else repeated it, and for those people it became a given.
But we never saw ourselves as a systemic party. We were always ready to be repressed, and there’s always repression, more of it or less of it.
— Until now, party leaders weren’t given actual prison time. That started in the summer of 2026.
— Look, party members of ours have been murdered. Farid Babaev, for one, was killed in the entryway of his apartment building in Dagestan. Yuri Shchekochikhin was poisoned in 2003. Those are the basics. Hardly anyone knows about them.
— Yabloko used to be seen as Yavlinsky’s party, and he personally made all the key decisions. Until recently, few people had even heard of the party chairman, Nikolai Rybakov. What role does Yavlinsky play in the party now?
— Yavlinsky has always been the party’s ideological leader and its engine — the one who puts the ideas into words. He came up with the slogan “For life, for peace and freedom, for a life without fear,” and now 14-year-olds across the country are repeating it. It’s a universal opposition slogan. Formally, our chairman is someone else, and our chairmen change.
— Why didn’t Yavlinsky run for president in 2024?
— Because there were no presidential elections in 2024 — in the sense that they never would have let Yavlinsky take part. With this State Duma election, that wasn’t as obvious, so we decided to run, partly to change the political climate.
Our participation [in the campaign] clearly achieved that in the end. Three months ago, the words “I’m for peace and freedom, I’m for a life without fear” would have sounded forbidden, marginal, and isolated. Just running in the campaign, short as it was, legitimized that message and showed millions of people they weren’t alone. The Kremlin understood that, which is why it removed us.
We were told: “You’re running to get 2%, and the Kremlin will be rubbing its hands with glee.” Well, look at us now — we’ve broken out of that marginal position.
— What was the logic behind Yabloko’s federal list? It’s either people known only locally or complete nobodies.
— Well, thanks a lot.
— You’re more the locally known type.
— I’m kidding. There was a simple answer to the authorities here. You jail our leaders, Maxim Kruglov and Shlosberg. You don’t let Rybakov or other well-known figures run. And you think that will bleed us dry. So look: out come these nobodies, as you call them. And millions of people immediately rally around those nobodies and support them, and their ratings climb. That tells you it’s not about the people — it’s about the values. People support the position, not specific last names.
And on the whole, if you look closely, everyone on the federal list is terrific. I like them a lot. They’re all really good at what they do, each in his own region and his own field. And yes, it happens that people in politics aren’t very well known, but that’s not their fault. Now they’ve become known — and I hope they’ll become better known still.
— Do you think they’ll let the party go on existing at all?
— That doesn’t depend on us, and the question shouldn’t concern us at all. We’ve spent the past few years guessing how much time we have left anyway. But institutionally, a party is just a way of working. A form. People can be brought together in plenty of ways. A party is more convenient, of course, because you can run in elections, have political resources, issue statements, and gather people around you safely.
We hope it survives, because the law gives us that right. And people in Russia have that right. We don’t know what decision will be made. It could be anything. The range of what could happen to Yabloko runs from the party being dissolved to our position becoming the cornerstone of the whole state.
— Has it become scarier to stay in Russia?
— I won’t say it hasn’t. Of course it’s scary. And not so much for me — my loved ones are the ones who are very scared.
I did an interview on Alexey Pivovarov’s show Redaktsiya [The Newsroom]. I always ask everyone up front whether they’re a “foreign agent” or have some other designation. He’s a “foreign agent,” but Redaktsiya isn’t, so they can publish anything. My relatives wrote to me right away: “Kirill, get yourself cut out of that video — that’s prison.”
That’s the state people are in right now in Russia — let alone party members. It’s scary, and my colleagues are probably scared too. But it will be scarier if Russia goes to hell and nothing can be done about it anymore. As long as there’s still a chance to do something, better to use it than to regret it later. That outweighs the fear.
— How do you define the goal of your work right now?
— The goal is for people to stop going to the front, stop shooting, stop dying. For them to stop being afraid they’ll be sent to the front — I mean mobilization — and to stop leaving their cities, their villages, and their country. For people to stop losing the ones they love.
That’s the main goal; everything else follows from it. We can see that our voice carries loudly enough that even without seats in the State Duma we can influence the political climate and the situation in the country.
We’ll keep working, but the goal isn’t personal careers or seats. It’s building a modern state that is safe both for its own citizens and for everyone else.
— Do you believe Yabloko can influence the decision on whether to carry out mobilization?
— Yes, I’m 100% sure of it, and this election showed it. It can — 100%, even 1,000%.
— How did the election show that?
— We gave voice to the mood of people who oppose mobilization, and the authorities certainly saw it. They’ll factor that into their policy.
— You were 17 when you joined Yabloko in 2010. Now other 17-year-olds are discovering the party. How has Yabloko changed since then?
— Yabloko has become more modern. Right now it’s the only opposition party that people with our views and values can join. It didn’t shut down, though there were a million reasons to — and credit for that goes to Yavlinsky, who was criticized for exactly the things he’s praised for today. Everyone used to say, “It’s long past time to shut Yabloko down. Why does it even exist?” And today it turns out Yabloko is a kind of Noah’s ark — a place where people who hold antiwar views can come together and not be afraid.
Who else but Yavlinsky could have carried that off? He did — and when they removed us from the election, I went to him and said I wanted to shake his hand. I’m genuinely glad he lived to see times like these in Yabloko. And that all of us did.
— Over all these years in the party, have you dealt with burnout?
— Of course I have, and it’s not some forbidden topic. Everyone deals with burnout. It’s just that at some point, working in Russia, you develop an immunity to it. It was hard not to burn out during the trial, for instance. We’re used to injustice, but injustice this blatant…
Back in 2019, we were collecting signatures for the Moscow City Duma election. Like many others, I wasn’t registered as a candidate, and we held rallies. One of our volunteers collected a signature for me from his grandmother. To keep me off the ballot, the Moscow City Election Commission started doctoring those signatures so it could rule them invalid.
They deliberately [changed] a six to an eight, for instance. And they declared the grandmother dead. We went to see her and recorded a video showing she was alive. It changed nothing, of course. But while we were filming, I got to know her and thanked her for her support. And she said to me: “When my grandson came around to get me to sign for you, I only signed because he’s my grandson. But after seeing how the authorities go after their opponents, you’re the only ones I’ll be supporting. This government considers me dead.”
What’s going on [now] is even more absurd than that was.
And back then, as much as I might have wanted to burn out, I understood that it was the starting point for something new and far more serious. The fact that they fight us so openly, so publicly, is an admission that we’re a real political alternative. And that motivates more than any burnout.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russia won't seriously consider peace while Ukraine lacks sufficient anti-ballistic capability
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said "Russia won’t seriously consider peace while Ukraine lacks sufficient anti-ballistic capability."
He said emergency services have been working since overnight at the sites of Russian strikes. "It was a massive strike - the Russians spent a long time preparing and combined different types of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones to inflict maximum damage on civilian infrastructure. There is destruction in Kyiv and the surrounding region, in Odesa region and in Chernihiv region," the president wrote on his Telegram channel on Thursday morning.
He said residential buildings in Kyiv were damaged, including an apartment building whose upper floors were destroyed, as well as a children’s hospital and a school. Emergency and rescue operations are continuing. As of now, this Russian strike is known to have killed 12 people in Kyiv, with one death in the surrounding region. About 40 more people were injured. In Odesa region, the enemy attacked a checkpoint on the border with Moldova with drones, and in Chernihiv region it struck gas infrastructure.
"Unfortunately, while Moscow is investing in ballistics and escalation, the world’s response to such strikes isn’t always what’s needed. And Russia won’t seriously consider peace while Ukraine lacks sufficient anti-ballistic capability," Zelenskyy stressed.
"We’re doing everything to ensure protection is there, and work is underway every day on the FREYJA program. But interceptors can’t yet replace Patriots, and they’re needed every day. Every additional missile saves the lives of our people. I thank everyone who understands this and is looking for and finding ways to help," the president wrote.

articles.title: Turkey says it will not fall into Israeli 'trap' in Syria
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey says it will not fall into Israeli 'trap' in Syria, denies military presence in air base
Turkey “will not fall into the trap” set by Israel, the country’s presidency said in a statement, days after Tel Aviv struck the Abu al-Duhur air base located near Aleppo.
"We are experienced enough not to fall into the trap of figures like (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu, who aim to undermine peace and stability in our region," said Burhanettin Duran, the Turkish presidency's director of communications.
After the site was struck, causing damage to its runways, reports said that a Turkish delegation had been at the site just hours earlier, but Turkey has denied a military visit to the location.
Israeli media said a Turkish military delegation had been at the site, and a Syrian monitor said the delegation was there as part of efforts to rehabilitate the base.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said Turkish forces had recently toured the base, warning that Israel would not tolerate a "threat" from a Turkish presence there.
"We will not tolerate a Turkish military entrenchment moving southward, because it threatens us," Netanyahu told an army radio podcast.
The premier's office also said on Tuesday evening that Israel had repeatedly warned Syria that deploying Turkish forces at an airbase near Aleppo would pose a threat to its national security, noting that Damascus had ignored the warnings.
The office stated that Israel and Syria had agreed to maintain the status quo on security matters, claiming that Damascus was on the verge of violating this understanding by allowing the Turkish military deployment.
But Turkish defence ministry spokesman Rear Admiral Zeki Akturk said the strikes were "unacceptable" and that Ankara would act "resolutely" to protect Syria's efforts to establish post-war stability.
"Israel's attack on the Abu al-Zuhur air base is aimed at harming Syria's stability, security, unity, integrity and infrastructure. Attacks violating Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity are unacceptable," he told journalists.
"In this context, our efforts and contributions to protect Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and help it establish a stable and secure environment, will continue resolutely."
Turkey’s presidency has also clarified that it is not considering retaliation.
Duran said that Netanyahu was "clinging to this irrational stance due to upcoming elections, internal political tensions, and fears. He views hostility toward Turkey as a political lifeline".
The development comes as Syria’s new transitional government has condemned the Israeli strikes, which marked the first time the location was targeted since the fall of the Assad regime.
The US has also rebuked the strikes, with US special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack describing the attack as an "unnecessary escalation" that did not serve regional stability.
Barrack pointed to the approach taken by the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, saying Damascus "has not adopted a hostile posture nor maintained proxy forces, but has repeatedly demonstrated a preference for de-escalation with Israel".
He also emphasised Washington's efforts to reduce tensions between the two countries.
Barrack called on all sides to prioritise "reasoned dialogue" over further military incidents.
Since the fall of the Assad regime, Israel has stepped up its raids and incursions into Syria, while targeting much of the country's remaining military infrastructure.
Israeli attacks have struck Syrian air-defence systems, long- and medium-range missiles, weapons and missile depots, scientific research centres and other military facilities.
Israeli strikes have also hit several key Syrian airfields and military installations, including Hama airport, as well as Tiyas, Shayrat, Palmyra, Dumayr and Mezzeh airfields.
Agencies contributed to this report.

articles.title: US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East, relieving long-deployed USS Lincoln
articles.body:
US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East, relieving long-deployed USS Lincoln
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Asia-based USS George Washington aircraft carrier is now operating in the Middle East, the U.S. military said Thursday, relieving a long-deployed carrier following reports of mental health challenges and supply shortages aboard while it was supporting the Iran war.
U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said on social media that the carrier arrived in the region Wednesday. It was not clear when the USS Abraham Lincoln would arrive back in the U.S. or whether it would make a port stop along the way, but the journey takes just over a month.
The Washington arrived as concerns have grown about the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment, which has included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 250 days, and about reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products.
Several Democratic lawmakers have pressed the Department of Defense for accountability over conditions aboard the Lincoln, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said were “completely misrepresented.”
Hegseth spoke with the Lincoln’s crew last week, and Adm. Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command, visited this past weekend. In an editorial published Sunday by The Wall Street Journal, Cooper said the crew “delivered a performance for the ages, and now you are going home.”
Extended deployments of carriers wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment. While renewed hostilities between the U.S. and Iran calmed in recent weeks, the Navy is enforcing a reimposed blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz, and the Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war.
Hegseth has said the U.S. can maintain the blockade “indefinitely.”
President Donald Trump this week downplayed reports about conditions on the Lincoln, which left its homeport in San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. Trump called the nearly nine months at sea that the sailors endured a “good period of time” but added that “over the years, we’ve had them out there much longer.”
Trump told reporters Monday that he spoke with a retired admiral over the weekend who recounted being on ships for “much longer.” Trump said the admiral assured him that the Lincoln is “beautifully maintained and beautifully taken care of.” Trump did not name the admiral.
In a statement Sunday after visiting the Lincoln, Cooper praised the carrier’s leaders for prioritizing mental health and resilience.
“History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era,” Cooper said.
The Washington joins the USS George H.W. Bush in the Middle East, leaving Asia without an American carrier strike group at a time when China has shown more signs of aggression.
The lack of a U.S. carrier in the Pacific may be short-lived if the Navy deploys another in the next couple of months. But it shows how the open-ended operations with Iran are running some American sailors ragged, analysts say, while the Trump administration further retreats from the Asia-Pacific region and focuses on the Western Hemisphere.

articles.title: Once again, Israeli air strikes are massacring people in Gaza
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What ceasefire? Once again, Israeli air strikes are massacring people in Gaza
Israel attacked the Gaza Strip after days of contacts and meetings aimed at advancing the fragile ceasefire to its next stage, raising renewed fears that the truce could collapse and the war could return on a wider scale.
At least 15 Palestinians were killed and dozens injured by two Israeli airstrikes on Gaza City within less than 24 hours.
The first, on Tuesday evening, hit a beachside café in the port area. The second, on Wednesday afternoon, hit a municipal police headquarters in the city centre, killing at least nine people and injuring around 15 others, according to Palestinian medical sources.
The strikes came as US, Egyptian and Qatari mediators intensified efforts to advance negotiations over the second phase of the ceasefire agreement.
The talks remain stalled over several fundamental issues, including an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza, Hamas's weapons, and the future administration and security of the territory.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has insisted that any future arrangement must guarantee Israel's security and has vowed that Israel would not leave Gaza.
Hamas, meanwhile, says the question of its disarmament cannot be separated from an end to the genocidal war, an Israeli withdrawal and guarantees that the agreement will be implemented.
Nine killed at police headquarters
At least nine Palestinians, including a woman, were killed on Wednesday afternoon when an Israeli airstrike struck the Hamas-run municipal police headquarters in central Gaza City.
The Gaza police force said Israeli aircraft targeted the headquarters, causing deaths and injuries.
Medical sources said some victims arrived at hospitals in pieces, while around 15 wounded people were being treated, several of them in critical condition.
Palestinian sources identified six of those killed as Brigadier General Abu Akram Jundiya, Colonel Abu Abdullah al-Hajin, Colonel Abu Khalil Tamraz, Major Abu Bilal Abu Sam'an, Colonel Abu Omar Aliyan and Colonel Faten al-Sahhar, who headed the women's police force in Gaza City. The identities of the remaining victims were still being verified.
Witnesses said the strike caused a powerful explosion and scattered shrapnel across the surrounding area.
The headquarters is located near a municipal park and tents sheltering displaced Palestinians, according to local sources.
Residents described scenes of panic following the blast, saying the area had been busy with civilian activity when the attack took place.
Gaza's Ministry of Interior and National Security accused Israel of carrying out a "brutal massacre" against members of the civilian police force and appealed to mediators and the international community to intervene.
"The occupation is working to dismantle the police force in order to spread chaos within Palestinian society," the ministry said.
Hamas described the strike as "a new Zionist war crime", saying it demonstrated the Netanyahu government's refusal to implement the ceasefire agreement and move towards its next phase.
The movement also rejected Israeli claims that attacks on police personnel were aimed at resistance leaders, calling such assertions a justification for targeting civilians and members of the police.
Less than a day earlier, another Israeli strike had killed six Palestinians at a café in Gaza City's port area.
Six people, including a child, were killed and 14 wounded when an Israeli airstrike hit the "Helwa wal Murra" café on Tuesday evening, according to Gaza's Ministry of Health and medical sources.
Ismail al-Thawabta, director general of Gaza's Government Media Office, said the victims were taken to al-Shifa Medical Complex.
Witnesses said the café was frequented by civilians and that the force of the explosion threw several people into the sea, prompting rescue teams to search the water.
The six killed were identified as Ezz El-Din Salem Deeb, Jihad Muhammad Hamdi Al-Masdi, Muhammad Hamdi Ahmad Al-Masri, Essam Muhammad Musa Murtaja, Muhammad Fathi Hussein Nasser and Samed Samir Harb Abu Habel.
The Israeli army claimed it had targeted "leaders in an elite Hamas unit during a meeting", including a company commander and three faction leaders.
It alleged that those targeted were involved in planning attacks against Israeli forces in Gaza and said one had participated in the 7 October 2023 attack.
A Hamas source, who preferred not to be named, told The New Arab that the members targeted at the café were unarmed and had been meeting as part of preparations to consolidate the movement's weapons and implement US President Donald Trump's plan.
The claim adds further sensitivity to the attack because Hamas's weapons remain one of the most contentious issues in negotiations over the next phase of the ceasefire.
Fears of more war
The recent increase in Israeli violence also extended beyond airstrikes. Local sources said an Israeli special forces unit carried out an operation in southern Gaza early Wednesday, arresting a senior Hamas police officer.
Witnesses in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis said a force of around 15 to 20 soldiers, accompanied by dogs, entered from the al-Shouka area and reached the tent of Colonel Sabri Abdelaal before arresting him along with Nash'at Za'arab, who works for a security company.
The force subsequently withdrew towards the Israeli-held "yellow line", according to the sources.
The operation, coinciding with the strike on the municipal police headquarters, has raised questions about Israel's approach to Gaza's security and police structures at a time when negotiators are discussing who will administer and police the territory during the next phase.
The recent violence occurred during a sensitive political time. US envoy Jared Kushner met Hamas officials in Cairo and then traveled to Israel for talks with Netanyahu, as Washington, Egypt, and Qatar urged parties to implement the second phase of the ceasefire.
Major disagreements remain: Israel demands Hamas's disarmament and security guarantees, while Hamas wants an end to the war and Israeli withdrawal before discussing weapons.
Netanyahu emphasises Israel's security, which Hamas sees as enabling future military action. Reports also say Netanyahu plans to meet opposition leader Yair Lapid to brief him on security issues amid mounting political and security pressures.
In Gaza, residents and analysts say the renewed attacks demonstrate how distant the language of ceasefire negotiations remains from reality on the ground.
Gaza-based political analyst Taysir Abdullah told TNA that Israel's use of high-explosive weapons in densely populated areas makes civilian casualties almost inevitable.
"What does the occupation expect when it launches a missile weighing a ton of explosives into the midst of displaced people's tents, whatever the justification or reason?" he said. "Yesterday, six were killed in Gaza's port, and today nine were killed in the municipal park. Does he think he's performing delicate surgery with a laser endoscope?"
"These are piles of tightly packed flesh. If you hit a small stone, you'd hit two or three people, so what about a missile?" he added.
Abdullah questioned whether the attacks could genuinely be described as targeted operations against wanted individuals, arguing that civilians continue to bear the consequences.
"These are massacres for which children, women, and the elderly pay the price daily," he said, warning that continued attacks during negotiations could undermine efforts to reach a durable agreement.
He also criticised Palestinian factions meeting in Cairo for what he described as passivity, urging them to take action rather than limiting themselves to statements of condemnation.
Between negotiations and bombardment
For Gaza's residents, the ceasefire remains an abstraction when explosions can return without warning.
"We don't understand how we can talk about a second phase, an agreement, and mediators, while at the same time we hear explosions and see people falling before our eyes," Gaza City resident Ibrahim Abu Shaaban told TNA.
"If negotiations are underway, who will stop the bombing? And who can guarantee that the agreement will hold if Israel can bomb whenever it wants?" he asked.
Another resident, Mohammed Odwan, said fear had returned to Gaza's streets.
"Every day we hear news about negotiations, then the bombing comes and kills people," he said. "For us, it makes no difference whether they say the war is over or it continues, as long as death reaches our tents, cafés and streets."

articles.title: Sweden Orders Strike Drones for Its Army for the First Time — Contract Awarded to Nordic Wing
articles.body:
Sweden has ordered strike drones for its armed forces for the first time. The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration has awarded a contract to Danish company Nordic Wing to supply the systems.
The report comes from SVT Nyheter.
The procurement is worth 350 million Swedish kronor ($37 million). The drones are scheduled to be delivered to the Swedish military in the second quarter of 2027.
The systems consist of the Astero ISR drone and Raptor 2 strike drones. They operate through shared software.
The reconnaissance drone is intended to detect targets, after which one or more strike drones can engage them.
The drones were purchased along with several control stations consisting of laptops and radio equipment. The order also includes simulators for operator training and specialized workshop containers for field maintenance.
According to the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration, the systems are primarily intended for the Army.
“This system provides new capabilities, particularly for light units, to engage targets at long distances and combat units that have very high effectiveness,” said Lennart Widerström, head of the Land Warfare School in Skövde.
He said Swedish troops are ready to receive the new drones and will be able to quickly begin using them for defense.
“We want this capability because it is a natural part of modern warfare,” Widerström said.
The Swedish Armed Forces say the procurement is only a first step. The country plans to procure unmanned systems from several different manufacturers in the future. The decision to order strike drones is also linked to lessons from the war in Ukraine, which the Swedish military is closely monitoring.
Drones made by Danish company Nordic Wing have been supplied to Ukraine’s Defense Forces for several years.

articles.title: Pirates hijack cargo ship carrying Turkish weapons off Somalia’s coast, official says
articles.body:
Pirates hijack cargo ship carrying Turkish weapons off Somalia’s coast, official says
MOGADISHU, Somalia (AP) — Pirates hijacked a Cameroon-flagged cargo ship off Somalia’s Puntland coast earlier this week and took the vessel, which was carrying Turkish weapons, toward the region’s Nugaal coast, a Somali official said Thursday.
The M/V LUTUF was seized on Monday about 3½ nautical miles off Marraya in Puntland’s Eyl district, the official told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity, because he wasn’t authorized to speak publicly about sensitive information.
The ship, owned by Polar Movement Shipping, was carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in Mogadishu, as well as communications and satellite equipment, the official said.
The 10-member crew included six Indians, one Turkish national, one Georgian and two Serbian security guards, he said.
There was no immediate comment from Turkish authorities about the incident.
Eight pirates, believed to be members of a group previously involved in the hijacking of the M/V Sward on April 26, took the vessel toward the coast near Garmaal in Puntland’s Dangoroyo district.
Two Turkish-owned vessels later approached the hijacked ship, while Turkish helicopters and drones monitored the area, the official said. On Tuesday, a small boat carrying two men approached the vessel and delivered khat, a stimulant commonly chewed in Somalia, he said.
After the boat returned to shore, an airstrike followed, killing four men and wounding two others, the official said.
The circumstances of the strike, including who carried it out and whether those killed were involved in the hijacking, couldn’t immediately be independently verified. The status of the LUTUF, including its crew and cargo, wasn’t immediately clear. The AP couldn’t independently verify all details of the account.
___
Suzan Fraser contributed to this report from Ankara, Turkey.

The Unmanned Systems Forces—established in June 2024 as the world's first military branch dedicated to unmanned systems—number about 15,000.

articles.title: Six UK pro-Palestine orgs demand end of arms trade to Israel
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
On anniversary of 'symbolic' Palestine recognition, UK groups demand end to Israel arms trade
With the first anniversary of Britain's official recognition of the State of Palestine approaching, six British pro-Palestinian organisations have stepped up pressure on the government, calling for an end to the arms trade with Israel, the suspension of military and intelligence support, and comprehensive sanctions against it.
The demands come alongside calls for British action that goes beyond political recognition to practical measures.
In a comment to The New Arab on Wednesday, 19 August, Chris Nineham, vice-president of the Stop the War Coalition, said Britain's recognition of Palestine "was welcome, but, as we feared, it was symbolic", adding, "The people of Palestine need action, and we are calling on our government to end British support for Israel immediately.
"We are working to organise another mass demonstration on 10 October to pressure it to take action."
Nineham's comments come as the organisations prepare to organise a new national march in central London next October, in an attempt to pressure the British government to take tougher steps towards Israel.
In a joint statement on Wednesday, the organisations said that "Palestinians in the Gaza Strip continue to face killing, hunger and displacement, while British-funded humanitarian aid remains subject to Israeli restrictions".
They called on the British government to work to halt Israeli attacks and ensure aid reaches the Strip without restrictions.
The demand to lift restrictions on aid coincides with a position Britain announced at the UN Security Council on 11 August, when it called on the Israeli authorities to end what it described as "unacceptable restrictions" on aid and allow safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access to Gaza.
'Britain must act'
The statement is titled, "Three years of genocide... Britain must act".
The signatories said their next march will take place on Saturday, 10 October, at noon in central London, coinciding with three years since the ongoing genocide in Gaza.
The official website of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign confirms the date and location of the march.
The statement was signed by the Palestinian Forum in Britain, the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, the Stop the War Coalition, the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, Friends of Al-Aqsa, and the Muslim Association of Britain.
The United Kingdom officially recognised the State of Palestine on 21 September 2025.
At the time, the government said that the decision aimed to revive hope for peace and a two-state solution.
But the organisations that signed the statement believe the recognition was not followed by British action at the required level.
They say "real action" requires ending arms trade with Israel and suspending military and intelligence support that they consider to contribute to facilitating violations of international law.
They also called for British companies, banks, universities and charities to be prevented from supporting activities linked to the occupation or settlements, starting with a ban on trade connected to Israel's illegal occupation and extending to comprehensive sanctions against Israel.
Britain suspended 29 export licences to Israel in September 2024 after concluding that there was a clear risk that the equipment covered by them could be used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law in Gaza.
The latest government data shows that six additional licences were subsequently suspended or amended as new information emerged.
The organisations expanded their demands to include the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, warning of continued settlement expansion, settler violence and restrictions on Al-Aqsa Mosque.
The British government, for its part, says Israeli settlements are illegal under international law.
It recently condemned the rise in settler violence and expressed concern about developments at the Noble Sanctuary in Jerusalem.
In June, London, in coordination with international partners, imposed sanctions on six entities and one individual, saying they were involved in financing, enabling or carrying out acts of settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
Britain also strengthened its guidance for British companies and citizens in June, explicitly advising them against engaging in economic or financial activities in Israeli settlements, which it considers illegal, while reaffirming its continued support for trade with Israel within its pre-1967 borders.
In their statement, the organisations said Britain's commitment to international law "cannot be held hostage to the Israeli electoral timetable", arguing that the time had come to move from political recognition of the Palestinian state to practical measures.
The organisers are calling for widespread participation in the 10 October march, in an attempt to put pressure back on the streets of Britain.
They also want to place the issues of arms, sanctions, trade and military support at the forefront of the debate over what has actually changed in British policy since the recognition of Palestine.

articles.title: Romania destroys naval drone near offshore gas platform
articles.body:
- Romania neutralized one maritime drone near the Neptun Deep gas platform on Thursday, hit first by an F-16 and later destroyed by EOD personnel.
- Authorities initially reported two separate drones before clarifying it was a single device that survived the F-16's cannon fire before being found and destroyed.
Romania neutralized a maritime drone near the Neptun Deep gas platform in the Black Sea on Thursday. Officials initially reported that two separate drones had been destroyed, but it was later established that only one drone was involved throughout the entire incident, according to Defense Minister Radu Miruță and Romanian President Nicușor Dan.
The drone was spotted several hundred meters from the platform’s gas extraction operations at around 6:28 a.m. local time, reported by a commercial vessel working in the area, according to Romania’s Ministry of National Defence. Two Romanian F-16s were scrambled, and one aircraft engaged the target with its onboard cannon. The drone was hit and damaged but not destroyed, and it continued drifting in the sea.
A Romanian Coast Guard vessel then arrived in the area to verify the results of the engagement. When the crew located the damaged drone, they initially believed they had found a second device. They had not. It was the same drone that had already been struck by the F-16, still drifting after surviving the initial hit. Romanian EOD personnel subsequently destroyed it completely.
Miruță said the drone was loaded with explosives and that Ukraine had officially confirmed through a recently established direct communication channel that it did not belong to Ukrainian forces.
The drone was found within Romania’s exclusive economic zone, roughly 80 nautical miles east of Constanța, near the offshore platform where several hundred people were working at the time.
President Dan congratulated the armed forces and the F-16 pilots, crediting the Coast Guard for its speed in reporting the drone’s presence.
“A race against time, in which the top priority was protecting the lives of the people working on the platform and keeping critical infrastructure out of any potential danger,” Dan said.
“I strongly condemn the escalation of these types of irresponsible incidents on the part of the Russian Federation,” Dan said. “We remain vigilant alongside our NATO allies to defend ourselves and repel such provocations.”
Thursday’s incident follows a pattern of drone activity around the Neptun Deep project in recent weeks. On August 11, Romanian Naval Forces divers destroyed two drifting drones near the same site through controlled detonation. Vice Admiral Mihai Panait, chief of the Naval Forces Staff, identified those as Gerbera-type drones of Russian production. On August 16, an explosive ordnance disposal team recovered a drone wing roughly 83 nautical miles east of Constanța. Romanian pilots first destroyed a drone over national territory on July 24.
Neptun Deep is operated by OMV Petrom, which holds a 50 percent stake alongside Romgaz. The project is scheduled to begin production in 2027 and is expected to make Romania the European Union’s largest natural gas producer.

articles.title: Bradley IFVs won battles in Ukraine. The parts to keep them running went out of production
articles.body:
The US Army Contracting Command—Detroit Arsenal has published a market survey seeking companies that can supply components for M2A2 ODS-SA Bradley infantry fighting vehicles (IFVs) headed to Ukraine—parts that original manufacturers have stopped making. The posting asks for firms with immediate access to the components or a realistic plan to restart their production, Militarnyi reported.
Maintaining Western armored vehicles in active combat has strained repair chains throughout the war, with licensing requirements and long lead times slowing restoration of battle-damaged equipment. When components go out of production entirely, the problem shifts from delayed repairs to no repairs at all.
Parts nobody makes
The survey targets components affected by what the command calls an aging manufacturing base. Original suppliers have discontinued production of multiple subsystems, including turret drive control units, transmission control modules, heater mounts, ammunition chutes, specialized Dialight Corp lens assemblies, and other structural, electrical, and mechanical parts unique to the M2A2 ODS-SA.
The posting is not a tender and does not guarantee a contract. Its stated goal is to identify companies that can either deliver the parts now or credibly restart production.
Restoring and sustaining Bradleys for Ukraine
The parts shortage creates a two-stage problem. Before Bradleys can be shipped to Ukraine, the US military refurbishes them at its depots—restoring each vehicle to combat-ready condition under a standard called Fully Mission Capable + Safety. Without the discontinued components, that refurbishment stalls.
The same parts are also needed to keep Bradleys already fighting in Ukraine on the road. The posting specifies that field servicing must proceed without delays caused by parts shortages—meaning the crisis affects both the pipeline into Ukraine and the fleet already there.
Potential contractors must demonstrate repair and technical validation capabilities, supply chain management, and the ability to quickly resume manufacturing of parts that no longer have a producer. The command requires a detailed transition plan with a timeline from contract signing to the delivery of the first restored vehicle.
The US also plans to involve the future contractor in training Ukrainian military mechanics. The contractor would develop courses, manuals, and provide specialized tools and equipment—including instruction on armored recovery vehicles.
The 25-mm cannon, stops T-72s, if the turret still turns
The M2 Bradley carries infantry into combat and mounts a 25-mm M242 Bushmaster cannon that fires up to 500 rounds per minute and can defeat Russian light armored vehicles and the side and rear armor of main battle tanks. The US has supplied more than 200 Bradleys to Ukraine under the previous administration, with combat losses mounting across multiple frontline sectors.
Separately, the US Army presented XM30 infantry fighting vehicle candidates at the Michigan Defense Expo 2026—the program is eventually designed to replace the Bradley.

articles.title: Defense Ministry, Armed Forces must develop practical solutions on mobilisation – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expects the Ministry of Defense and the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) to provide concrete solutions and proposals regarding mobilization, contract service, and the rotation of military personnel.
"Everything related to mobilization and contracts, everything related to the rotation of our soldiers – we need concrete solutions and concrete proposals. I very much look forward to systematic joint work in this area by the Armed Forces and the Ministry of Defense," Zelenskyy said while introducing Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara on Thursday.
He also called for a more humane and systematic approach to resolving organizational issues within the military.
According to the president, one of the biggest challenges for the defense sector right now is a lack of financial resources.
"We need to find the necessary resources, and I believe this is the greatest challenge we’ve ever faced. The war has become more expensive, and that’s a fact. We need more resources; the shortfall is greater," Zelenskyy said.
He said Russia is using more tools in the war against Ukraine, so it is necessary not only to defend ourselves but also to take more active measures.
"All of this requires resources. This must also be a joint effort by the entire state," the president said.

articles.title: Germany to provide 50 million euros to repair Chornobyl Nuclear Plant after Russian strike
articles.body:
Rescuers inspect the damaged Safe Confinement of the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant after a Russian drone attack in Prypiat, Ukraine, on Feb. 14, 2025. (Yan Dobronosov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
Germany will provide 50 million euros to repair a protective structure over Ukraine's Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant, Ukraine's Energy Ministry said on Aug. 19.
The structure, called the New Safe Confinement, had previously been damaged by a Russian drone strike.
Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal thanked German Environment, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety Minister Carsten Schneider for his recent visit to the plant and commitment to "ensuring the nuclear safety of Ukraine and all of Europe."
The funds will be deposited into the International Cooperation Account for Chornobyl (ICCA), according to the Energy Ministry.
The New Safe Confinement, a protective shelter covering the remains of Chornobyl's destroyed reactor, was damaged by Russian drones in February 2025.
The incident was confirmed after the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated the damage at 500 million euros.
The steel structure was designed to shield the reactor for 100 years, yet it remained fully functional for only six, as the waterproof inner membrane smoldered for three weeks after the strike, forcing firefighters to cut holes in the outer layer.
Ukraine's other partners, including the European Union and Norway, have also promised to deposit funds into the ICCA to assist in the structure's repair.

The attack has killed at least 15 people and injured dozens more, along with damage to a kindergarten, children's hospital, apartment buildings, and food warehouses.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that during the daytime attacks, a critical infrastructure facility in Kyiv was "deliberately targeted" for the first time in several months.

Oleh Klots, former director general of the state-owned Medical Procurement of Ukraine, will serve as interim head of the agency pending the appointment of a permanent successor by Ukraine's new defense minister, according to Arsen Zhumadilov.

articles.title: Russia strikes Kyiv twice in one day, killing at least 17, as Zelensky vows a ‘long-range’ response
articles.body:
Russia strikes Kyiv twice in one day, killing at least 17, as Zelensky vows a ‘long-range’ response
Russia struck Kyiv with drones again on the evening of August 20 — after a massive combined attack the night before.
At around 5:30 p.m. local time, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that falling drone debris started a fire in an office building in the capital’s Holosiivskyi district. He later specified that a second fire had broken out in a nonresidential area. The attack killed two people and injured at least two more.
The Kyiv City Administration warned that air quality in the Holosiivskyi district was temporarily worse due to the strike and advised residents to close their windows and limit their time outdoors.
In his evening address, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine “will definitely respond to Russia for this strike, just as it has for other strikes.” He said the response would be “just and long-range.”
Overnight into August 20, Russia launched a combined strike on Kyiv that Zelensky described as among Russia’s most cynical, calculated, and large-scale attacks. At least 15 people were killed in that attack, and dozens of buildings were damaged, including homes, a school, and a kindergarten.

articles.title: Russia strikes food warehouses in Boryspil, Kyiv Oblast
articles.body:
Russia strikes food warehouses in Boryspil, Kyiv Oblast

                20 August, 10:39

                                                        Food warehouses and Red Cross facilities have been damaged in Boryspil as a result of a Russian attack on the night of 19-20 August, with firefighters still tackling blazes at the sites of the strikes.
Source: Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi
Details: In addition to Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, Russian forces attacked civilian infrastructure in Odesa and Chernihiv oblasts overnight.

articles.title: North Korea fires possible ballistic missile toward sea
articles.body:
North Korea fires 10 short-range ballistic missiles
August 20, 2026
North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea on Thursday, South Korea's military said.
Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said the North fired the missiles "from its Pyongyang area."
Earlier, the Japanese prime minister's office and the country's Coast Guard also said they detected the suspected launch.
The incident came hours after US President Donald Trump said he would meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un later this year.
US-South Korea military drills shortened
The latest missile launches also come as South Korea and the US continue military drills that are set to end Friday after Trump's order to significantly reduce US participation.
Pyongyang has long denounced US-South Korea joint exercises as invasion rehearsals, often responding with missile launches.
Trump described the war games as "inappropriate and hostile," on Wednesday as he announced he would meet Kim later this year,
"These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been president, has been unthreatening and respectful," he wrote on Truth Social.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of Kim Jong Un, dismissed Trump’s move, saying, "The provocative, aggressive nature of the drills won't change even though their duration and size were reduced."
"If the US calculates that it can propagate its recent measure as the one of so-called good faith, they will not get the desired answer," she added.
